Exposé V
COHOMOLOGY IN TOPOIby J. L. Verdier
Introduction

In this exposé we present the elementary commutative cohomological invariants of topoi. In no. 1, we study flat modules and flat morphisms of ringed topoi. The proofs are given under the hypothesis, most often satisfied in practice, that the topoi have enough points (IV 6). These proofs are taken up again in the general case in Appendix 8, where Deligne, using the technique of local inductive limits, moreover generalizes to the case of topoi D. Lazard's theorem on the structure of flat modules. The theorems of this exposé are existence theorems for spectral sequences relating the various cohomological invariants (nos. 3, 5, 6). It is known that, even for topological spaces, Čech cohomology does not in general coincide with sheaf cohomology [11]. In Appendix 7 we introduce a modified Čech calculus which makes it possible to obtain, by means of coverings, the cohomology of sheaves in an arbitrary topos. In this appendix we are led to use simplicial coverings (hypercoverings), whose homotopy invariants have been studied in [1] (cf. also [17]).

The cohomological invariants introduced are elementary in the sense that we do not use derived categories [12]. The reader familiar with this language will immediately translate the various statements of this exposé and will then be able to generalize them to complexes and to hypercohomology. Moreover, this language of derived categories is used in the sequel to this seminar.

We restrict ourselves here to commutative cohomology. For non-commutative \(H^1\), used in this seminar, and for non-commutative \(H^2\), we refer to [9]. The functors that we derive are additive; we remain silent on multiplicative structures (cf. [7]).
0. Generalities on abelian categories
In this section we recall some lemmas, most of which are to be found in [11].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 0.1

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an abelian category possessing a generator. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The category \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfies axiom AB 5): small direct sums are representable, and if \((X_i)\), \(i \in I\), is a small increasing filtered family of subobjects of an object \(X\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(Y\) is a subobject of \(X\), then \[ \Bigl(\sup_i X_i\Bigr) \cap Y = \sup_i (X_i \cap Y). \]

  2. ii)

    Small pseudo-filtered inductive limits (I 2.7) are representable and commute with finite projective limits.

Moreover, if the above conditions are satisfied, small filtered inductive limits are universal (I 2.6).

Proof: It is clear that (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i). To show that i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii), and to prove the additional assertion, it suffices to use the fact that \(\mathcal{A}\) is a full subcategory of a category of modules \(\mathcal{M}\) over a suitable ring, such that the inclusion functor \(u : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{M}\) has an exact left adjoint \(v\) [5]. The verification is then trivial.

It is known [11] that an abelian category \(\mathcal{A}\) possessing a generator and satisfying axiom AB 5) has enough injectives, i.e., every object embeds in an injective object. Moreover, by the result already cited [5], small products are representable in \(\mathcal{A}\) (axiom AB 3\(^*\))).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 0.2

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(\mathcal{A} \underset{u}{\overset{v}{\leftrightarrows}} \mathcal{B}\) two adjoint functors (\(u\) is left adjoint to \(v\)). Consider the two properties:

  1. i)

    The functor \(u\) is exact.

  2. ii)

    The functor \(v\) carries injective objects of \(\mathcal{B}\) to injective objects of \(\mathcal{A}\).

1) We always have the implication (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii).

If, moreover, every nonzero object of \(\mathcal{B}\) is the source of a nonzero morphism into an injective object, then (ii) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (i).

2) Suppose that:

  1. a)

    the category \(\mathcal{B}\) has enough injectives.

  2. b)

    one of the two equivalent conditions (i) and (ii) above is satisfied.

  3. c)

    the functor \(u\) is faithful.

Then the category \(\mathcal{A}\) has enough injectives.
Proof: The proof is left to the reader.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 0.2.1

The category of commutative groups has enough injectives. Applying lemma 0.2, we deduce that every category of unital modules over a ring with a unit element has enough injectives. Applying then the result of [5] (used in the proof of 0.1) and 0.2, we deduce that every abelian category possessing a generator and exact small filtered inductive limits has enough injectives; this gives a new proof of this fact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 0.3

Let \(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\mathcal{C}\) be three abelian categories and \(u : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}\), \(v : \mathcal{B} \to \mathcal{C}\) two additive left exact functors. Suppose that \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) have enough injective objects. The following two properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    There exists a spectral functor whose term \(E_2^{p,q}\) is: \[ R^p v R^q u \] and which abuts to \(R^{p+q} vu\) (suitably filtered).

  2. ii)

    The functor \(u\) carries injective objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) to objects acyclic for the functor \(v\).
Proof: (i) \(\Longrightarrow\) (ii) is trivial, since it suffices to apply the spectral functor to an injective object. The implication (ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) (i) is proved in [11].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 0.4

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{B}\) be two abelian categories and \(u : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}\) an additive left exact functor. Let \(M\) be a subset of the set of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) possessing the following properties:

  1. 1)

    Every object of \(\mathcal{A}\) embeds in an element of \(M\).

  2. 2)

    If \(X \oplus Y\) belongs to \(M\), the object \(X\) belongs to \(M\).

  3. 3)

    If \[ 0 \longrightarrow X' \longrightarrow X \longrightarrow X'' \longrightarrow 0 \] is an exact sequence and if \(X'\) and \(X\) belong to \(M\), then \(X''\) belongs to \(M\) and the sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow u(X') \longrightarrow u(X) \longrightarrow u(X'') \longrightarrow 0 \] is exact. The zero objects belong to \(M\).

Then every injective belongs to \(M\), and the objects of \(M\) are acyclic for \(u\), i.e., for every \(q \neq 0\) and every object \(X\) of \(M\), we have \(R^q u(X) = 0\). (In particular, resolutions by objects of \(M\) make it possible to compute the derived functors of \(u\).)
For the proof see [11] 3.3.1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 0.5

Let \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) be two universes, \(\mathcal{A}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{B}\)) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-category) that is abelian, satisfies axiom AB 5) relative to \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. to \(\mathcal{V}\)), and possesses a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small (resp. \(\mathcal{V}\)-small) generating family. Let \(\varepsilon : \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{B}\) be an exact, fully faithful functor. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. 1)

    There exists a generating family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) such that the family \((\varepsilon(X_i))_{i \in I}\) is generating in \(\mathcal{B}\).

  2. 1')

    Every object of \(\mathcal{B}\) is isomorphic to a quotient of an object of the type \(\bigoplus_{\alpha \in A} \varepsilon(Y_\alpha)\) where \(A \in \mathcal{V}\).

Under these conditions, we have the following property:

  1. 2)

    \(\varepsilon\) carries \(\mathcal{U}\)-small products to products (hence commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small projective limits).

Moreover, under the equivalent conditions 1) or 1'), the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. a)

    For every object \(Y\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), every subobject of \(\varepsilon(Y)\) is isomorphic to the image under \(\varepsilon\) of a subobject of \(Y\).

  2. a')

    There exists a generating family \((X_i)_{i \in I}\) of \(\mathcal{A}\) such that the family \((\varepsilon(X_i))_{i \in I}\) is generating in \(\mathcal{B}\) and such that for every \(i \in I\), every subobject of \(\varepsilon(X_i)\) is isomorphic to the image under \(\varepsilon\) of a subobject of \(X_i\).

  3. b)

    Every object of \(\mathcal{B}\) is isomorphic to a subobject of an object of the type \(\prod_{\alpha \in A} \varepsilon(Y_\alpha)\) where \(A \in \mathcal{V}\).

  4. c)

    \(\varepsilon\) commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small direct sums (hence commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small inductive limits).

Moreover, under conditions 1) and a') we have:

  1. d)

    \(\varepsilon\) carries injective objects to injective objects.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 0.5.1

When \(\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{V}\) in 0.5, conditions 1) and a') imply that \(\varepsilon\) is an equivalence of categories (since we then have b), 2), and a)).

We shall confine ourselves to giving indications of the proof. The implications 1) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) 1'), 1) \(\Longrightarrow\) 2), are left to the reader. It is clear that a) \(\Longrightarrow\) a'). Let us show that a') implies d). Let \(M\) be an injective in \(\mathcal{A}\). For every \(i \in I\) and every subobject \(Y \hookrightarrow X_i\) of \(X_i\), the homomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}(X_i, M) \to \operatorname{Hom}(Y, M)\) is surjective. Hence, by virtue of a') and the full faithfulness of \(\varepsilon\), for every subobject \(U \hookrightarrow \varepsilon(X_i)\), the homomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}(\varepsilon(X_i), \varepsilon(M)) \to \operatorname{Hom}(U, \varepsilon(M))\) is surjective. Since the \(\varepsilon(X_i)\) form a generating family of \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\varepsilon(M)\) is injective [11]. Let us show that a') \(\Longrightarrow\) b). By enlarging the family of the \(X_i\) if necessary, we may assume that for every \(i \in I\), every quotient of \(X_i\) is isomorphic to some \(X_j\) for a suitable \(j\). Then let, for every \(i \in I\), \(X_i \hookrightarrow M_i\) be a monomorphism into an injective object. The family \((\varepsilon(X_i))_{i \in I}\) is stable under quotients, and for \(i \in I\), the morphism \(\varepsilon(X_i) \hookrightarrow \varepsilon(M_i)\) is, by d), a monomorphism into an injective object. One then verifies immediately that, since the family \(\varepsilon(X_i)\) is generating, the family \((\varepsilon(M_i))_{i \in I}\) is cogenerating, whence b). Let us show that b) \(\Longrightarrow\) c). Let \((Z_\alpha)_{\alpha \in A}\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small family of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) and let us show that the canonical morphism \[ \bigoplus_{\alpha \in A} \varepsilon(Z_\alpha) \longrightarrow \varepsilon\Bigl(\bigoplus_{\alpha \in A} Z_\alpha\Bigr) \] is an isomorphism. Since the family of objects \(\varepsilon(Y)\) is cogenerating, it suffices to show that for every object \(Y\) of \(\mathcal{A}\), the homomorphism \[ \operatorname{Hom}\Bigl(\varepsilon\bigl(\textstyle\bigoplus_\alpha Z_\alpha\bigr), \varepsilon(Y)\Bigr) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}\Bigl(\textstyle\bigoplus_\alpha \varepsilon(Z_\alpha), \varepsilon(Y)\Bigr) \] is an isomorphism, which follows from the full faithfulness of \(\varepsilon\). It remains to show that c) \(\Longrightarrow\) a). Let \(Z\) be a subobject of \(\varepsilon(Y)\). By virtue of 1'), there exists a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small family \(Y_\alpha\) of objects of \(\mathcal{A}\) and an epimorphism from \(\bigoplus \varepsilon(Y_\alpha)\) onto \(Z\). Since \(\varepsilon\) commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small direct sums, there is therefore an epimorphism \(\varepsilon(Y') \to Z\). Let us denote by \(u : \varepsilon(Y') \to Z \to \varepsilon(Y)\) the composite morphism. We have \(Z = \operatorname{Im}(u)\). Since \(\varepsilon\) is fully faithful, we have \(u = \varepsilon(v)\) and hence \(Z = \operatorname{Im}(\varepsilon(v)) = \varepsilon(\operatorname{Im}(v))\).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 0.5.2.

Let \(\operatorname{Sex}_{\mathcal{V}}(\mathcal{A})\) be the category of contravariant functors from \(\mathcal{A}\) to the category of commutative \(\mathcal{V}\)-groups which commute with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small inductive limits. Show that under conditions 1) and a') the canonical functor from \(\mathcal{B}\) to \(\operatorname{Sex}_{\mathcal{V}}(\mathcal{A})\) is an equivalence.
1. Flat modules

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos (IV 11.1.1). A right (resp. left) \(A\)-Module \(M\) is said to be flat if the functor \(M \otimes_A -\) (resp. \(- \otimes_A M\)) from the category of left (resp. right) \(A\)-Modules to the category of abelian sheaves of \(E\) is exact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.2

Let \(M\) be a \(B\text{-}A\) bi-Module.

  1. 1)

    The following properties are equivalent:

    1. i)

      The module \(M\) is left \(A\)-flat.

    2. ii)

      For every injective \(B\)-Module \(I\), the left \(A\)-Module \(\mathscr{H}om_B(M, I)\) is injective.

  2. 2)

    A Module \(M\) that is a pseudo-filtered inductive limit (I 2.7.1) of flat Modules is flat.

  3. 3)

    Finally, if \(M_\bullet = \dots M_{i+1} \to M_i \dots\) is an acyclic complex of flat modules (\(M_i = 0\) for \(i < i_0\)), then for every Module \(F\), the complex: \[ M_\bullet \otimes_A F = \dots M_{i+1} \otimes_A F \longrightarrow M_i \otimes_A F \dots \] is acyclic.

Proof: By (IV 12.12) we have an adjunction isomorphism: \[ \operatorname{Hom}_B(M \otimes_A -, -) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Hom}_A(-, \mathscr{H}om_B(M, -)) . \] It then suffices to apply 0.2 to obtain the equivalence (i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (ii). This adjunction isomorphism moreover shows that the tensor product commutes with inductive limits. The fact that pseudo-filtered inductive limits are exact (0.1) yields the second assertion. To show that the complex \(M_\bullet \otimes_A F\) is acyclic, it suffices to show that for every injective abelian sheaf \(I\) the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf{Z}}(M_\bullet \otimes_A F, I)\) is acyclic. This complex is isomorphic, by the adjunction formulas, to the complex \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(F, \mathscr{H}om_{\mathbf{Z}}(M_\bullet, I))\). Now by the equivalence (i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) (ii), the complex of sheaves \[ \mathscr{H}om_{\mathbf{Z}}(M_\bullet, I) \] is an acyclic complex whose objects are injective, whence the conclusion.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3.1

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(H\) an object of \(E\), \(M\) a flat \(A_{/H}\)-Module. Then \(j_{H!} M\) is a flat \(A\)-Module. In particular \(A_H\) is flat on the right and on the left.

Suppose, to fix ideas, that \(M\) is a right \(A_{/H}\)-Module. For every left \(A\)-Module \(P\), we have a canonical isomorphism (IV 12) \[ P \otimes_A j_{H!} M \simeq j_{H!}(P \otimes_{A_{/H}} M) . \] The functors \(j_{H!}\) and \(j_H^*\) are exact (IV 11.3.1 and 11.12.2), and by hypothesis the functor \(- \otimes_{A_{/H}} M\) is exact. Hence the functor \(P \longrightarrow P \otimes_A j_{H!} M\) is exact, and \(j_{H!} M\) is flat.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.3.2 (Projection formula for closed immersions)

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(i : F \to E\) a closed subtopos of \(E\). Set \(i^*A = A_{/F}\). For every (right) \(A_{/F}\)-Module \(M\) and every (left) \(A\)-Module \(P\), we have a functorial isomorphism \[ i_*(M \otimes_{A_{/F}} i^*P) \simeq (i_*M) \otimes_A P . \]

Let \(U\) be the open complement of \(F\) and \(j : U \to E\) the canonical immersion. We have \(j^*(i_*M \otimes_A P) \simeq 0 \otimes_{A_{/U}} j^*(P)\) (IV 12); hence \(i_*M \otimes_A P\) has its support in \(F\). Therefore the adjunction morphism \(i_*M \otimes_A P \to i_*i^*(i_*M \otimes_A P)\) is an isomorphism (IV 14). We have \(i^*(i_*M \otimes_A P) \simeq i^*i_*M \otimes_{A_{/F}} i^*P\) (IV 12), and since \(i : F \to E\) is a closed immersion, \(i^*i_*M \simeq M\) (IV 14); whence the announced isomorphism.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.3.3

For every flat \(A_{/F}\)-Module \(M\), \(i_*M\) is flat.
It follows from 1.3.2 and from (IV 14) that the functor \(P \longmapsto (i_*M) \otimes_A P\) is an exact functor.

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(x : P \to E\) a point of \(E\) (IV 6.1), \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\) the category of neighbourhoods of \(x\) (IV 6.8). To every object \(V\) of \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\) corresponds an object of \(E\), again denoted \(V\), and a point \(x_V : P \to E/V\) of \(E/V\). Moreover, to every morphism \(u : V \to W\) of \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\), corresponds an essentially commutative diagram of morphisms of topoi (IV 6.7)
(1.4.1) \[ \xymatrix{ P \ar[r]^{x_V} \ar[dr]_{x_W} & E/V \ar[d]^{j_u} \\ & E/W } \]
Let \(N\) be an \(A_x\)-module (resp. a set). From the diagram (1.4.1), we deduce a diagram of \(A_x\)-modules (resp. of sets):
(1.4.2) \[ \xymatrix{ x_W^* x_{W*}N \ar[r]^-{\mathrm{ad}_W} \ar[d]_{\phi(u)} & N \\ x_V^* x_{V*}N \ar[ur]_{\mathrm{ad}_V} & } \]

where \(\mathrm{ad}_W\) and \(\mathrm{ad}_V\) are the adjunction morphisms. Moreover, one verifies immediately that \(\phi(uv) = \phi(v)\,\phi(u)\). We thus have a functor from the filtered category \(\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ\) to the category of \(A_x\)-modules (resp. sets) and a homomorphism:
(1.4.3) \[ \Lambda(N) : \varinjlim_{V \in \mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} x_V^* x_{V*}N \longrightarrow N \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.5

For every \(A_x\)-module (resp. set) \(N\), \(\Lambda(N)\) is an isomorphism.

This proposition is a special case of a proposition due to Deligne (8.2.6). Let us give a direct proof of it. By passing to the underlying sets, it suffices to prove the proposition when \(N\) is a set (I 2.8). The cofiltered category \(\mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x))\) of arrows of \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\) is fibred over the category \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\) by the functor \(p : \mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x)) \to \mathrm{vois}(x)\) which assigns to an arrow its target. Let \(D\) be a category and \(F : \mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x)) \to D\) a pro-object (I 8.10). For every object \(V\) of \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\), let us denote by \(F_V\) the pro-object obtained by restricting the functor \(F\) to the fibre category \(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V\). To every morphism \(m : U \to V\) of \(\mathrm{vois}(x)\), the base change functor by \(m\) associates a morphism from the pro-object \(F_U\) to the pro-object \(F_V\), and the canonical morphisms of pro-objects \(F \to F_V\) determine a morphism of pro-objects:
(1.5.1) \[ F \longrightarrow \varinjlim_{V \in \mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} F_V \]
which one immediately verifies to be an isomorphism. Let us apply this remark to the pro-object of pointed sets:
(1.5.2) \[ (U, V, m) \longmapsto x_V^*(m) = F(U, V, m) . \]
We obtain an isomorphism of pro-objects:
(1.5.3) \[ F \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} \varinjlim_{(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V)^\circ} x_V^*(m) ; \]
whence, for every set \(N\), a bijection

(1.5.4) \[ \varinjlim_{\mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x))^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(m), N) \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} \varinjlim_{(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(m), N) . \]

But, for fixed \(V\), \(\varinjlim_{(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(m), N)\) is identified with \(x_V^* x_{V*}N\). Indeed, we have \(x_V^* x_{V*}N \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x_V)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}_{E/V}(W, x_{V*}N)\) by IV 6.8.1, so, by adjunction, we have \(x_V^* x_{V*}N \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x_V)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(w), N)\), and moreover the category \(\mathrm{vois}(x_V)\) is equivalent to the category \(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V\) (IV 6.7.2). Finally, the canonical transition maps \[ \varinjlim_{(\mathrm{vois}(x)/U)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_U^*(m), N) \longrightarrow \varinjlim_{(\mathrm{vois}(x)/V)^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(n), N) \] in 1.5.4 are identified with the canonical maps \(x_U^* x_{U*}N \longrightarrow x_V^* x_{V*}N\) (1.4.3), as the reader will readily verify. We thus have a bijection
(1.5.5) \[ \varinjlim_{\mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x))^\circ} \operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(m), N) \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} x_V^* x_{V*}N \]

and the map \(\Lambda(N) : \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} x_V^* x_{V*}N \longrightarrow N\) (1.4.3) composed with the bijection 1.5.5 arises from the maps \(\operatorname{Hom}(x_V^*(m), N) \longrightarrow N\) which assign to a map \(r : x_V^*(m) \longrightarrow N\) the image under \(r\) of the marked point of \(x_V^*(m)\). To prove the proposition, it then suffices to observe that every object \((U, V, m)\) of \(\mathrm{Fl}(\mathrm{vois}(x))\) is bounded below by \((U, U, \mathrm{id}_U)\) and that \(x_U^*(\mathrm{id}_U)\) reduces to a single element, or, in other words, that the canonical morphism from the constant pro-object reduced to a single element to \(F\) is an isomorphism of pro-objects.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.6

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(M\) an \(A\)-Module.

  1. 1)

    When \(M\) is flat, for every point \(x : P \to E\) of \(E\), the \(A_x\)-module \(M_x\) is flat.

  2. 2)

    Let \((x_i)_{i \in I}\) be a conservative family of points of \(E\) such that for every \(i \in I\), \(M_{x_i}\) is a flat \(A_{x_i}\)-module.

Then \(M\) is flat.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1.6.1

Let \(M\) be a flat Module and \(V\) an object of \(E\). The \(A_{/V}\)-Module \(j_V^* M\) is flat.

We must show that the functor \(P \longmapsto P \otimes_{A_{/V}} j_V^* M\) is exact. Since the extension-by-zero functor \(j_{V!}\) is exact and faithful (IV 11.3.1), it suffices to show that the functor \(P \longmapsto j_{V!}(P \otimes_{A_{/V}} j_V^* M)\) is exact. We have a functorial isomorphism \(j_{V!}(P \otimes_{A_{/V}} j_V^* M) \simeq j_{V!}(P) \otimes_A M\) (IV 12.11), and hence the functor \(P \longmapsto j_{V!}(P) \otimes_A M\) is exact (IV 11.3.1).

Let us prove 1). Suppose, to fix ideas, that \(M\) is a flat left \(A\)-Module and let \(x : P \to E\) be a point of \(E\). Let us show that the functor \(N \longmapsto N \otimes_{A_x} M_x\) from the category of right \(A_x\)-modules to the category of commutative groups is exact. For this it suffices to show that this functor is left exact. With the notation of 1.4, let \(V\) be a neighbourhood of \(x\) and \(j_V : E/V \to E\) the localization morphism. We have, for every \(A_x\)-module \(N\), \[ x_V^* x_{V*}N \otimes_{A_x} M_x \simeq x_V^* x_{V*}N \otimes_{A_x} x_V^*(j_V^* M) \simeq x_V^*(x_{V*}N \otimes_{A_{/V}} j_V^* M) \] (IV 12.11). Hence the functor \(N \longmapsto x_V^* x_{V*}N \otimes_{A_x} M_x\) is left exact. Consequently, the functor \(N \longmapsto N \otimes_{A_x} M_x\), a filtered inductive limit of left exact functors (1.5), is left exact. Let us prove 2). Let \[ 0 \longrightarrow P' \longrightarrow P \longrightarrow P'' \longrightarrow 0 \] be an exact sequence of \(A\)-Modules and let us show that the sequence \(0 \to P' \otimes_A M \to P \otimes_A M \to P'' \otimes_A M \to 0\) is exact. For this it suffices to show that for every \(i \in I\), the sequence obtained by passing to the fibres at \(x_i\) is exact (IV 6). Now the sequence of fibres at \(x_i\) is the sequence (IV 13.5) \[ 0 \longrightarrow P'_{x_i} \otimes_{A_{x_i}} M_{x_i} \longrightarrow P_{x_i} \otimes_{A_{x_i}} M_{x_i} \longrightarrow P''_{x_i} \otimes_{A_{x_i}} M_{x_i} \longrightarrow 0 \] and since \(M_{x_i}\) is flat, this sequence is exact.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.7

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(u : E' \to E\) a morphism of topoi, and set \(A' = u^*A\). Let \(M\) be a right (resp. left) \(A'\)-Module. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. i)

    The functor \(N \longmapsto M \otimes_{A'} u^*N\) (resp. \(N \longmapsto u^*N \otimes_{A'} M\)) from the category of left (resp. right) \(A\)-Modules to the category of abelian sheaves of \(E'\) is exact.

  2. ii)

    \(M\) is a flat \(A'\)-Module.

It is clear that ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i). Let us show that i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii). We shall give the proof only in the case where \(E'\) has a conservative family of points \((x_i)_{i \in I}\). The general case is treated in (8.2.7). In this particular case, which covers most of the applications, we are reduced to the case where \(E'\) is the punctual topos and where, consequently, the morphism \(u\), which we shall denote by \(x\), is a point of \(E\) (1.6 and IV 11.3.1). We shall confine ourselves to the case where \(M\) is a right \(A'\)-Module. The case where \(M\) is a left \(A'\)-Module reduces to this one by passing to opposite rings. Let \(V\) be a neighbourhood of \(x\) and \(V_x\) its fibre at \(x\). We have, with the notation of 1.4, an essentially commutative diagram of morphisms of topoi:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ P \ar[r]^{j} \ar[dr]_{x_V} & P/V_x \ar[r]^{j_{V_x}} \ar[d]^{x/V} & P \ar[d]^{x} \\ & E/V \ar[r] & E } \]

where \(x/V\) is the morphism deduced from \(x\) by localization on \(V\) (IV 5.10) and \(j\) is the morphism deduced from the marked point of \(V_x\). Let us show that the functor \(N' \longrightarrow M \otimes_{A'} x_V^*N'\) is exact. We have \(x_V^* = j^*(x/V)^*\) and \(\mathrm{id} = j^* j_V^*\), and hence we have a canonical isomorphism \(M \otimes_{A'} x_V^*N' \simeq j^*(j_{V_x}^* M \otimes_{A'_{/V}} (x/V)^*N')\). Since the functor \(j^*\) is exact and since the functor \(j_{V_x!}\) is exact and faithful (IV 11.3.1), it suffices to show that the functor \(N' \longmapsto j_{V_x!}(j_{V_x}^* M \otimes (x/V)^*N')\) is exact, and hence (IV 12.11), it suffices to show that the functor \(N' \longmapsto M \otimes_{A'} j_{V_x!}(x/V)^*N'\) is exact. But it follows from the definition of the inverse image of an induced topos (IV 5.10.2) that \(j_{V_x!}(x/V)^*N'\) equals \(x^* j_{V!}N'\), and since the functor \(j_{V!}\) is exact (IV 11.3.1), the functor \(N' \longmapsto M \otimes_{A'} x^* j_{V!}N'\) is exact by hypothesis. For every \(A'\)-module \(Q\), we have a functorial isomorphism (1.5): \[ Q \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \varinjlim_{\mathrm{vois}(x)^\circ} x_V^* x_{V*}Q . \] By the above, the functor \(Q \longmapsto M \otimes_{A'} Q\) is a filtered inductive limit of left exact functors. It is therefore left exact, and hence \(M\) is flat.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.7.1

Let \(u : (E', A') \to (E, A)\) be a morphism of ringed topoi, \(M\) a flat \(A\)-Module. Then \(u^*M\) is a flat \(A'\)-Module.
This follows from the criterion given in 1.7 and from the formula (IV 13.4.5).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1.7.2

Let \(u : (E', A') \to (E, A)\) be a morphism of ringed topoi. The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. i)

    the right (resp. left) \(u^{-1}(A)\)-Module \(A'\) is flat.

  2. ii)

    the functor \(u^*\) from the category of left (resp. right) \(A\)-Modules to the category of left (resp. right) \(A'\)-Module is exact.
The equivalence follows from 1.7 and from the definition of \(u^*\) (IV 13.2.1).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.8

A morphism of ringed topoi that possesses the equivalent properties of 1.7.2 is called a left flat morphism of topoi (resp. right).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.9

Let \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) be two universes, \(C\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the categories of \(\mathcal{U}\)- and \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves of sets respectively, \(\varepsilon : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the canonical inclusion functor, \(A\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf of rings on \(C\).

  1. 1)

    The functor \(\varepsilon\) commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small inductive and projective limits of Modules. The functor \(\varepsilon\) is conservative and fully faithful on the categories of Modules.

  2. 2)

    For every object \(H\) of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\), there is a canonical isomorphism \(\varepsilon(A_H) \simeq \varepsilon(A)_{\varepsilon(H)}\).

  3. 3)

    Every left or right injective \(A\)-Module is carried by \(\varepsilon\) to an injective \(\varepsilon(A)\)-Module.

  4. 4)

    Every right or left flat \(A\)-Module is carried by \(\varepsilon\) to a flat \(\varepsilon(A)\)-Module.

  5. 5)

    The functor \(\varepsilon\) commutes with the formation of the tensor product and of the sheaf of homomorphisms.

The formation of the associated sheaf does not depend on the universe (II 3.6). It follows then from the construction of inductive and projective limits in categories of sheaves (II 4.1 and 6.4) that the functor \(\varepsilon\) commutes with \(\mathcal{U}\)-small projective limits of sets or of Modules, whence 1). Let us prove 2). By taking a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small generating subcategory of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\), we may reduce to the case where \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small (III 4.1). It then follows from (II 6.5) that the free \(A\)-Module generated by \(H\) is obtained by forming the presheaf of free \(A\)-modules generated by \(H\), a formation which commutes with enlargement of universes, and then forming the associated sheaf, an operation which likewise commutes with enlargement of universes (II 3.6). To prove 3) it suffices to show, by virtue of 0.5, that every sub-\(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaf of a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf, which is quite clear. Let us prove 4). Let \(M\) be a flat \(A\)-Module. It suffices to show that for every injective \(\varepsilon(A)\)-Module \(J\), the abelian sheaf \(\mathscr{H}om_{\varepsilon(A)}(\varepsilon(M), J)\) is injective (1.2). By virtue of 0.5, \(J\) is a subobject, hence a direct summand, of an object of the type \(\prod_\alpha \varepsilon(I_\alpha)\), where the \(I_\alpha\) are injective. We may therefore assume that \(J = \varepsilon(I)\) where \(I\) is an injective object. If the homomorphism \(\varepsilon(\mathscr{H}om_A(M, I)) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_{\varepsilon A}(\varepsilon M, \varepsilon(I))\) is an isomorphism, we deduce that \(\mathscr{H}om_{\varepsilon(A)}(\varepsilon(M), \varepsilon(I))\) is injective by 3). It remains, then, to prove 5). The fact that the formation of the tensor product commutes with the functor \(\varepsilon\) follows from IV 12.6 and from the fact that the formation of the associated sheaf commutes with enlargement of the universe (II 3.6). For every object \(X\) of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) and every pair of \(A\)-Modules \(M\) and \(N\) of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) we thus have \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}}(\varepsilon X, \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}}(X, \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_A(\mathbf{Z}_X \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} M, N) \] by virtue of the full faithfulness of \(\varepsilon\), and then \[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(\mathbf{Z}_X \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} M, N) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\varepsilon A}(\varepsilon(\mathbf{Z}_X \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} M), \varepsilon N) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\varepsilon A}(\varepsilon\mathbf{Z}_X \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} \varepsilon M, \varepsilon N) \] by virtue of the full faithfulness of \(\varepsilon\) and of the above. Using then 2) and IV 12.14, we obtain in the end an isomorphism \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}}(\varepsilon X, \varepsilon\mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}}(\varepsilon X, \mathscr{H}om_{\varepsilon A}(\varepsilon M, \varepsilon N)) ; \] whence the announced isomorphism.

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) a small family of morphisms with the same target. For every finite set \(\Delta_n = [0, \dots, n]\), set \[ S_n(\mathcal{U}) = \coprod_{f : \Delta_n \to I} U_{f(1)} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(n)} , \] the sum being taken over the set of maps from \(\Delta_n\) to \(I\). Let \(m\) and \(n\) be two integers, \(g : \Delta_m \to \Delta_n\) a map. We define a morphism
(1.10.1) \[ s(g) : S_n(\mathcal{U}) \to S_m(\mathcal{U}) , \]

as follows: for every \(f : \Delta_n \to I\), the restriction of \(s(g)\) to \(U_{f(1)} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(n)}\) is the composite morphism of the canonical inclusion \[ U_{f(g(1))} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(g(m))} \longrightarrow S_m(\mathcal{U}) , \] and the unique morphism \[ s_f(g) : U_{f(1)} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(n)} \longrightarrow U_{f(g(1))} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(g(m))} \] such that for every \(i \in \Delta_m\) \[ \operatorname{pr}_{f(g(i))} s_f(g) = \operatorname{pr}_{f(gi)} \] (\(\operatorname{pr}_\alpha\) denotes the \(\alpha\)-th projection). We thus obtain a contravariant functor \(\Delta_n \longmapsto S_n\) from the category of finite sets to \(E\); in other words, a semi-simplicial complex \(S_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) of objects of \(E\). Note that this complex is canonically augmented toward \(X\). Every functor from \(E\) to a category \(C\) carries \(S_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) to a simplicial object of \(C\). In particular, if \(A\) is a Ring of \(E\), the functor "free \(A\)-Module generated" carries \(S_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) to a simplicial complex of \(A\)-biModules augmented toward \(A_X\) and denoted \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\). We have
(1.10.2) \[ A_n(\mathcal{U}) = \bigoplus_{f : \Delta_n \to I} A_{U_{f(1)} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{f(n)}} . \]
This complex will often be denoted

(1.10.3) \[ \xymatrix@C=3.5em{ \dots \ar@<1ex>[r]^{s_0} \ar[r]|{s_1} \ar@<-1ex>[r]_{s_2} & \bigoplus_{i,j} A_{U_i \times_X U_j} \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^{s_0} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_{s_1} & \bigoplus_i A_{U_i} \ar[r] & A_X } \]

where the arrows of 1.10.3 (except the last, which is the augmentation) represent the face operators of the simplicial complex \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\), that is, the morphisms corresponding to the increasing injective maps from \(\Delta_n\) to \(\Delta_{n+1}\) (\(s_i\) omits the integer \(i\)). To the complex \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) we associate a differential complex augmented toward \(A_X\):
(1.10.4) \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \dots \ar[r]^-{d} & \bigoplus_{i,j} A_{U_i \times_X U_j} \ar[r]^-{d} & \bigoplus_i A_{U_i} \ar[r] & A_X } \]
by setting

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.11

When the family \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) is epimorphic, the differential complex 1.10.4 is acyclic and provides a resolution of \(A_X\).

Let \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}\) denote the constant sheaf with value \(\mathbf{Z}\). By definition of the functor "free \(A\)-Module generated", we have, for every object \(H\) of \(E\), \[ A_H \simeq \underline{\mathbf{Z}}_H \otimes_{\underline{\mathbf{Z}}} A , \] whence \[ A_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \simeq \underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \otimes_{\underline{\mathbf{Z}}} A . \] Since the components of \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) are flat \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}\)-Modules ((1.3.1)), it suffices to prove the proposition when \(A = \underline{\mathbf{Z}}\).

Suppose first that \(E\) is the topos of sets. Then the augmented complex \(S_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) is a direct sum of augmented complexes of the type \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \dots \ar@<1.5ex>[r] \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-1.5ex>[r] & S \times S \times S \ar@<1ex>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<-1ex>[r] & S \times S \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & S \ar[r] & \{e\} } \] (\(\{e\}\) a set with one element). Each of these augmented complexes is homotopically trivial. Hence \(S_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) is a homotopically trivial augmented complex, and consequently its homology is trivial, whence the proposition in this case.

Now let \(p : \mathrm{Ens} \to E\) be a point of \(E\). Since the formation of the complex \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) commutes with the inverse image functors under morphisms of topoi, \(p^*(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U})) \simeq \underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(p^*(\mathcal{U}))\) is a resolution of \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{p^*X} \simeq p^*(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_X)\); whence the proposition when \(E\) has enough fibre functors (IV 4.6). This is the case in particular when \(E\) is a topos of presheaves \(\widehat{C}\), since for every object \(X\) of \(C\), \(\Gamma(X, -)\) is a fibre functor. In the general case, \(E\) is equivalent to a topos of sheaves on a small site \(C\) (IV 1), and the epimorphic family \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) is the image, under the functor "associated sheaf", of an epimorphic family \(\mathcal{U}' = (U'_i \to X')_{i \in I}\). Hence \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \simeq a\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_\bullet(\mathcal{U}')\) is a resolution of \(a\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{X'} \simeq \underline{\mathbf{Z}}_X\).
2. Čech cohomology. Cohomological notation
2.1 General notation

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(M, N\) two \(A\)-Modules (left, to fix ideas). We denote by \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; M, N)\) the value at \(N\) of the \(q\)-th right derived functor of the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(M, \cdot)\) [11]. The functors \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; M, N)\), \(q \in \mathbf{N}\), form a \(\delta\)-functor in the variable \(N\). It is also a contravariant \(\delta\)-functor in the variable \(M\). We have, by definition, \(\operatorname{Ext}^0_A(E; M, N) = \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N)\).

Let \(X\) be an object of \(E\). When \(M = A_X\), the free \(A\)-Module generated by \(X\) (IV 12), we set \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; A_X, N) = H^q(X, N)\). Note that in this new notation, the ring \(A\) no longer appears. This cannot cause confusion, since we shall show (3.5) that the formation of \(H^q(X, \cdot)\) commutes with restriction of scalars. The functor \(H^q(X, \cdot)\) is the \(q\)-th right derived functor of the functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(A_X, \cdot) = \operatorname{Hom}_E(X, \cdot)\), also denoted \(\Gamma(X, \cdot)\). When \(M = A\), we set \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; A, N) = H^q(E, N)\).
2.2 Localization.

Let \(X\) be an object of \(E\), \(j : E_{/X} \to E\) the localization morphism (IV 8). The functor \(j_X^*\) for Modules is exact (4.11) and has an exact left adjoint functor \(j_{X!}\) (4.11). Hence it carries injective Modules to injective Modules. We thus have, for a variable \(A\)-Module \(N\) of \(E\) and a variable \(A|X\)-Module \(M\) of \(E_{/X}\), functorial isomorphisms
(2.2.1) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A|X}(E_{/X}; M, j_X^* N) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; j_{X!}M, N) . \]
In particular, we have canonical isomorphisms \[ H^q(E_{/X}, j_X^* N) \simeq H^q(X, N) . \] For every object \(X\) of \(E\) and every pair \(M\) and \(N\) of \(A\)-Modules, we set:
(2.2.2) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M, N) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A|X}(E_{/X}; M|X, N|X) . \]

By the above, the functors \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M, \cdot)\) are the derived functors of the functors \(N \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{A|X}(M|X, N|X)\). The functors \((M, N) \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M, N)\), \(q > 0\), form a \(\delta\)-functor with respect to each of the variables.
2.3 The case of topoi of presheaves. Cohomology of a covering.

Let \(C\) be a small category equipped with a presheaf of rings \(A\), let \(\widehat{C}\) be the topos of presheaves on \(C\), and let \(X\) be a representable object of \(\widehat{C}\). The functor that assigns to an \(A\)-Module \(M\) the group \(\Gamma(X, M) = M(X)\) is exact (I 3). Consequently \(H^q(X, M) = 0\) for every \(q > 0\) and every \(A\)-Module \(M\), or equivalently \(A_X\) is a projective \(A\)-Module.

Let \(S\) be a presheaf on \(C\). For every \(A\)-Module \(M\) we have a canonical isomorphism (I 2): \[ \Gamma(S, M) \simeq \varprojlim_{C/S} M|S \] Moreover, for every injective \(A\)-Module \(M\), the \(A|S\)-Module \(M|S\) is injective (2.2). Consequently, the groups \(H^q(S, M)\) are the values at \(M|S\) of the right derived functors of the functor \(\varprojlim_{C/S}\). Denoting by \(\varprojlim^q_{C/S}\) these derived functors, we have canonical isomorphisms: \[ H^q(S, M) \overset{\sim}{\to} \varprojlim{}^q_{C/S} M|S . \] In particular, we have canonical isomorphisms \[ H^q(\widehat{C}, M) \overset{\sim}{\to} \varprojlim{}^q_{C} M . \]

Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and let \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), be a family of morphisms of \(C\) such that for every \(i \in I\), \(U_i \to X\) is squarable (I 10). Let \(A_\bullet\) denote the simplicial complex studied in 1.10: \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ A_\bullet = \dots \ar@<1ex>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<-1ex>[r] & \coprod_{(i,j) \in I \times I} A_{U_i \times_X U_j} \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & \coprod_{i \in I} A_{U_i} . } \] For every \(A\)-Module \(M\), we set \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, M) = \operatorname{Hom}_A(A_\bullet, M)\):

(2.3.3.1) \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, M) : \prod_{i \in I} M(U_i) \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & \prod_{(i,j) \in I \times I} M(U_i \times_X U_j) \ar@<1ex>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<-1ex>[r] & \dots . } \]
We set \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, M) = H^q(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, M))\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.4
  1. 1)

    With the notation of 2.3.3, let \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be the sieve generated by the family \((U_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\). We have a canonical isomorphism \[ H^q(\mathcal{U}, M) \simeq H^q(R, M) . \]

  2. 2)

    The functors \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, \cdot)\) commute with restriction of scalars.

Since \(R\) is a subobject of \(X\) in \(\widehat{C}\), the fibre products \(U_{i_1} \times_R U_{i_2} \times_R \dots \times_R U_{i_n}\) and \(U_{i_1} \times_X U_{i_2} \times_X \dots \times_X U_{i_n}\) are canonically isomorphic. It follows from 1.11 that the complex \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) is a resolution of \(A_R\), and from 2.3.1 that the components of \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) are projective Modules. The cohomology groups of \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, M)\) are therefore canonically isomorphic to \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(\widehat{C}; A_R, M)\), whence the isomorphism. Assertion 2) follows immediately from the description of \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, M)\) (2.3.3.1).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.5

Let \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X, i \in I)\) and \(\mathcal{U}' = (U'_j \to X, j \in J)\) be two families of morphisms with target \(X\); let \(\varphi = (\varphi : I \to J, m_i : U_i \to U'_{\varphi(i)})\) and \(\varphi' = (\varphi' : I \to J, m'_i : U_i \to U'_{\varphi'(i)})\) be two morphisms (over \(X\)) from \(\mathcal{U}\) to \(\mathcal{U}'\). The morphisms \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi'\) induce the morphisms \(\varphi^q\) and \(\varphi'^q\): \(\varphi'^q : H^q(\mathcal{U}', M) \longrightarrow H^q(\mathcal{U}, M)\). The morphisms \(\varphi^q\) and \(\varphi'^q\) are equal. In particular, if the families \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{U}'\) are equivalent (i.e. if there exist a morphism from \(\mathcal{U}\) to \(\mathcal{U}'\) and a morphism from \(\mathcal{U}'\) to \(\mathcal{U}\)), then the \(A\)-Modules \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, M)\) and \(H^q(\mathcal{U}', M)\) are canonically isomorphic.

Proof: Indeed, let \(R\) and \(R'\) be the sieves of \(X\) generated by the families \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{U}'\). The morphisms \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi'\) define one and the same morphism from \(R\) to \(R'\), and hence induce two homotopic morphisms between the projective resolutions \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) and \(A_\bullet(\mathcal{U}')\).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 2.3.6 (Standard resolution)

a) Let \(C\) be a small category. For every integer \(n > 0\), we denote by \(\operatorname{Fl}^n(C)\) the set of sequences of morphisms of \(C\): \((u_1, \dots, u_n)\) such that for every \(i\), \(0 < i < n\), the target of \(u_i\) equals the source of \(u_{i+1}\), so that the morphisms \(u_i\) and \(u_{i+1}\) are composable. Define a semi-simplicial set \[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \operatorname{ES}(C) = \operatorname{ob} C & \operatorname{Fl}^1(C) \ar@<0.5ex>[l] \ar@<-0.5ex>[l] & \operatorname{Fl}^2(C) \ar@<1ex>[l] \ar[l] \ar@<-1ex>[l] & \operatorname{Fl}^3(C) \ar@<1.5ex>[l] \ar@<0.5ex>[l] \ar@<-0.5ex>[l] \ar@<-1.5ex>[l] & \dots \ar[l] } \] whose face operators \(s_i : \operatorname{Fl}^n(C) \to \operatorname{Fl}^{n-1}(C)\) are the following: \[ \begin{aligned} s_0(u_1, \dots, u_n) &= (u_2, \dots, u_n) , \\ s_i(u_1, \dots, u_n) &= (u_1, \dots, u_{i+1}u_i, \dots, u_n) , \quad 0 < i < n , \\ s_n(u_1, \dots, u_n) &= (u_1, \dots, u_{n-1}) . \end{aligned} \]

b) Show that when \(C\) has an initial object or a final object, the complex \(\operatorname{ES}(C)\) is homotopically trivial.

c) For every object \(X\) of \(C\), we denote by \({}_X\backslash C\) the category of arrows with source \(X\). Define a semi-simplicial presheaf \(\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)\) whose value at every object \(X\) of \(C\) is \(\operatorname{ES}({}_X\backslash C)\). We denote by \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)}\) the free abelian semi-simplicial presheaf generated by \(\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)\). It is equipped with a canonical augmentation \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)} \longrightarrow \underline{\mathbf{Z}}\) into the constant presheaf with value \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}\). Show that, on passing to the associated differential complex, the complex \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)}\) is a resolution of \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}\) and that the components of this complex are projective abelian presheaves.

d) For every abelian presheaf \(M\), we set \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(M) = \operatorname{Hom}(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)}, M)\). Make explicit the components of \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(M)\). Show that for every integer \(q \geqslant 0\), \(H^q(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(M)) = H^q(\widehat{C}, M)\).

e) Show that for every sheaf \(S\) on \(C\), the functors \(H^q(S, \cdot)\) commute with restriction of scalars.

f) Observe that when \(C\) is a group, \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)}\) is the standard resolution of the trivial module \(\mathbf{Z}\) [3].

g) Show that for every abelian presheaf \(M\) on \(C\), \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)} \otimes M\) is a (left) resolution of \(M\). Define the functor \(\varinjlim_C\) on presheaves. Show that it is right exact. Denote its left derived functors by \(H_q(C, M)\). Show that the components of the complex \(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)} \otimes M\) are acyclic for \(\varinjlim_C\). Deduce from this, denoting by \(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(M)\) the complex \(\varinjlim_C(\underline{\mathbf{Z}}_{\underline{\operatorname{ES}}(C)} \otimes M)\), isomorphisms \(H_q(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(M)) \sim H_q(C, M)\).

h) Let \(u : \widehat{C} \to \mathrm{Ens}\) be the unique morphism from the topos \(\widehat{C}\) to the punctual topos. We denote by \(u_! : \widehat{C}_{\mathbf{Z}} \to \mathrm{Ab}\) the left adjoint of the functor \(u^* : \mathrm{Ab} \to \widehat{C}_{\mathbf{Z}}\). Show that for every abelian presheaf \(M\), \(u_!M = \varinjlim_C M\).

i) From now on we denote by \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(C, M)\) and \(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(C, M)\) the complexes denoted \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(M)\) and \(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(M)\). A presheaf \(M\) on \(C\) is said to be locally constant if it transforms every morphism of \(C\) into an isomorphism. Associate to every locally constant presheaf \(M\) a locally constant presheaf \(\check{M}\) on the category \(C^\circ\) (the category opposite to \(C\)) such that for every morphism \(u\) of \(C\), \(\check{M}(u) = M(u)^{-1}\). Find a canonical isomorphism between the complexes \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(C, M)\) and \(\operatorname{ST}^\bullet(C^\circ, \check{M})\) (resp. \(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(C, M)\) and \(\operatorname{ST}_\bullet(C^\circ, \check{M})\)).

j) Let \(C\) be a small category possessing an initial object (resp. a small filtered category). Show that for every constant presheaf \(M\), \(H^q(\widehat{C}, M) = 0\) for \(q > 0\) (resp. \(H_q(C, M) = 0\) for \(q > 0\)).
2.4 The case of small sites. Čech cohomology.

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, let \(\widetilde{C}\) be the topos of sheaves on \(C\), and let \(\varepsilon : C \to \widetilde{C}\) be the canonical functor that assigns to an object of \(C\) the sheaf associated to the presheaf represented by that object. By abuse of notation, for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every sheaf of \(A\)-modules \(M\) we shall set \(H^q(X, M) = H^q(\varepsilon X, M)\) (cf. 2.3.1). Recall that when the topology of \(C\) is coarser than the canonical topology, which is always the case in practice, the functor \(\varepsilon\) is fully faithful and allows one to identify \(C\) with its image under \(\varepsilon\).

We denote by \(\mathscr{H}^0 : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_A\) the inclusion functor of sheaves of \(A\)-modules into the category of presheaves of \(A\)-modules. Thus for every sheaf of \(A\)-modules \(M\) we have by definition:

for every object \(X\) of \(C\). The functor \(\mathscr{H}^0\) is left exact. Its right derived functors are denoted \(\mathscr{H}^q\). Since for every object \(X\) of \(C\) the functor "section over \(X\)" is exact in the category of presheaves, we have
for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every sheaf of \(A\)-modules \(M\), so that the presheaf \(\mathscr{H}^q(M)\) is none other than the presheaf \(X \longmapsto H^q(X, M)\).

We assume that \((C, A)\) is a small ringed site, so that \(\widetilde{C}\) is a topos to which the results of 2.3 can be applied. Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(R \hookrightarrow X\) a covering sieve. For every presheaf of \(A\)-modules \(G\), the groups \(H^q(R, G)\) (which are therefore computed in the topos \(\widehat{C}\)) are called the Čech cohomology groups of the presheaf \(G\) relative to the covering sieve \(R\).

When \(R \hookrightarrow X\) is the sieve generated by a covering family \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) of squarable morphisms, these groups can be computed by means of the complex \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, G)\) (2.3.3), called the Čech complex of \(G\) relative to the covering family \(\mathcal{U}\) (or to the covering \(\mathcal{U}\)). The groups \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, G) = H^q(R, G)\) (2.3.4) are then called Čech cohomology groups of \(G\) relative to the covering family \(\mathcal{U}\).

Let \(M\) be a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(C\). The groups \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{H}^0(M))\) are most often denoted, abusively, \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, M)\), and called Čech cohomology groups of the sheaf \(M\) relative to the covering family \(\mathcal{U}\).

We denote by \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^0 : \widehat{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_A\) the natural extension to presheaves of \(A\)-modules of the functor \(L\) described in II. Thus we have, by definition, for a presheaf \(G\) and an object \(X\) of \(C\):
(2.4.5.1) \[ \check{\mathscr{H}}^0(G)(X) = \varinjlim_{R \hookrightarrow X} G(R) , \]

the inductive limit being taken over the sieves covering \(X\). It follows from (2.4.5.1) that the functor \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^0\) is left exact. The right derived functors of \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^0\) are denoted \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^q\). Since the functors "section over \(X\)" and "filtered inductive limit" are exact, it follows from (2.4.5.1) that we have
(2.4.5.2) \[ \check{\mathscr{H}}^q(G)(X) = \varinjlim_{R \hookrightarrow X} H^q(R, G) , \]
the limit being taken over the sieves covering \(X\).
The presheaves \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^q\) are called the Čech cohomology presheaves. For every object \(X\) of \(C\), we set
(2.4.5.3) \[ \check{H}^q(X, G) = \check{\mathscr{H}}^q(G)(X) . \]

The groups \(\check{H}^q(X, G)\) are called the Čech cohomology groups. When the topology of \(C\) is defined by a pretopology, which is most often the case in practice, we have, taking 2.3.4 into account,
(2.4.5.4) \[ \check{H}^q(X, G) \simeq \varinjlim_{\mathcal{U}} H^q(\mathcal{U}, G) , \]
the inductive limit being taken over the squarable covering families preordered by the natural order relation on the sieves that correspond to them (2.3.5).
Let \(M\) be a sheaf of \(A\)-modules. We set, abusively
(2.4.6.1) \[ \check{H}^q(X, M) = \check{H}^q(X, \mathscr{H}^0(M)) , \qquad \check{\mathscr{H}}^q(M) = \check{\mathscr{H}}^q(\mathscr{H}^0(M)) , \]

and the groups \(\check{H}^q(X, M)\) are called Čech cohomology groups of the sheaf \(M\). Let us point out that, although the functors \(\check{H}^q\) are derived functors on the category of presheaves, they do not in general form a \(\delta\)-functor on the category of sheaves.
2.5 Change of universe. Čech cohomology in the case of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sites

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\). The site \((C, A)\) is then a \(\mathcal{V}\)-site, and we have a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\), a \(\mathcal{V}\)-topos \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\), and a canonical inclusion functor \(\varepsilon : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\). The functor \(\varepsilon\) is exact and fully faithful on the categories of Modules, and transforms injective Modules into injective Modules (1.9). Thus for every pair of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves of \(A\)-modules we have canonical isomorphisms
(2.5.1.1) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}; M, N) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}; \varepsilon M, \varepsilon N) \qquad q \geqslant 0 . \]
In particular, for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf of sets \(R\) on \(C\), we have canonical isomorphisms (2.1.1)
(2.5.1.2) \[ H^q(R, M) \simeq H^q(\varepsilon R, \varepsilon M) \qquad q \geqslant 0 , \]
and, still more particularly, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), we have canonical isomorphisms (2.4.1)
(2.5.1.3) \[ H^q(X, M) \simeq H^q(X, \varepsilon M) . \]

Loosely speaking, one may therefore say that the cohomology of sheaves does not depend on the choice of universe, and one may always, when a proof or a construction requires it, enlarge the universe in order to compute the cohomology of a sheaf.

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\). Let us denote by \(\widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{U}}\) the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves, and by \(\hat{\varepsilon} : \widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{U}} \to \widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}\) the inclusion functor of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves into the \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves of \(A\)-modules. The functor \(\hat{\varepsilon}\) is exact, and consequently the derived functors of the functor \(\hat{\varepsilon}\mathscr{H}^0 : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}\) ( ) are the functors \(\hat{\varepsilon}\mathscr{H}^q\), \(q \geqslant 0\). By abuse of notation, we shall again denote by \(\mathscr{H}^q : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}\), \(q \geqslant 0\), the functors \(\hat{\varepsilon}\mathscr{H}^q\). When \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, this enlargement of the universe offers the following advantage: The category \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is not in general a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, and the \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves of \(A\)-modules are not necessarily submodules of injective \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves, whereas the category of \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves is a topos (a \(\mathcal{V}\)-topos) and consequently every \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf of \(A\)-modules is a subobject of an injective \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf (0.1.1). Thus for every \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf of sets \(R\) (and in particular when \(R\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf) and for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf of \(A\)-modules \(M\), the groups \(H^p(R, \mathscr{H}^q(M))\) are defined by 2.1.1, and it follows from (2.5.1.2) that these groups do not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{V}\) under consideration. Similarly, for every pair of integers \(\geqslant 0\) \(p\) and \(q\), the presheaves \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^p(\mathscr{H}^q(M))\) are defined by 2.4.5, and it follows from (2.5.1.2) and (2.4.5.4) that these presheaves do not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{V}\) used to define them.

pages.title: 3. The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence relative to a covering

blocks.html: 3. The Cartan-Leray spectral sequence relative to a covering

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\). The functor \(\mathscr{H}^0 : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}\) (2.5.2) transforms the injective \(A\)-Modules into injective presheaves. For every integer \(q > 0\) and every \(A\)-Module \(M\), the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(\mathscr{H}^q(M)\) is zero.

Let \(a_{\mathcal{V}}\) denote the "associated sheaf" functor for \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves, and \(\varepsilon : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widetilde{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}\) the inclusion functor of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves into \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves. We have \(a_{\mathcal{V}} \mathscr{H}^0 = \varepsilon\) (II 3.6), and since the functors \(a_{\mathcal{V}}\) and \(\varepsilon\) are exact, we have \(a_{\mathcal{V}} \mathscr{H}^q = 0\) for every integer \(q > 0\). For every \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf \(M\) and every \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf \(N\) we have a functorial isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}}(N, \mathscr{H}^0(M)) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_{\widetilde{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}}(a_{\mathcal{V}} N, \varepsilon M)\). When \(M\) is injective, \(\varepsilon M\) is injective (1.9), and since the functor \(a_{\mathcal{V}}\) is exact, the functor \(N \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat{C}_{A,\mathcal{V}}}(N, \mathscr{H}^0(M))\) is exact. Consequently \(\mathscr{H}^0(M)\) is injective.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 3.2

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, \(R\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf of sets on \(C\), and \(M\) a sheaf of \(A\)-Modules. There exists a spectral sequence, functorial in \(R\) and in \(M\): \[ \text{(3.2.1)} \qquad H^{p+q}(aR, M) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p(R, \mathscr{H}^q(M)) . \] (When \(C\) is not \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, the term \(H^p(R, \mathscr{H}^q(M))\) must be interpreted as the cohomology of the presheaf \(\mathscr{H}^q(M)\) in the topos \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\), where \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(C\) is \(\mathcal{V}\)-small (2.5.2).)

By definition of the "associated sheaf" functor (cf. II), we have a functor isomorphism \(H^\bullet(aR, M) \simeq H^0(R, \mathscr{H}^0(M))\). The functor \(\mathscr{H}^0\) transforms injective objects into injective objects. The spectral sequence of the composed functors (0.3) is the desired spectral sequence.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3

Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\) and \(\mathcal{U} = (U_i \to X)\), \(i \in I\), a covering family such that for every \(i \in I\), the morphism \(U_i \to X\) is squarable. We then have a spectral sequence (called the Cartan-Leray spectral sequence): \[ \text{(3.3.1)} \qquad H^{p+q}(X, M) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{H}^q(M)) . \]

Let \(R \hookrightarrow X\) be the sieve generated by \(\mathcal{U}\). Since this sieve is covering, the sheaf associated to \(R\) is the sheaf associated to \(X\) (II 5.2). Taking 2.4.1 into account, we have \(H^{p+q}(aR, M) = H^{p+q}(X, M)\). The corollary then follows from 2.3.4.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.4

There exists a spectral sequence functorial in the sheaf \(M\) and the object \(X\) of \(C\) \[ \text{(3.4.1)} \qquad H^{p+q}(X, M) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = \check{H}^p(X, \mathscr{H}^q(M)) . \]
This spectral sequence yields, as \(X\) varies in \(C\), the spectral sequence of presheaves:
(3.4.2) \[ \mathscr{H}^{p+q}(M) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = \check{\mathscr{H}}^p(\mathscr{H}^q(M)) . \]
These spectral sequences yield functorial morphisms (edge morphisms):
(3.4.3) \[ \varphi^q(M) : \check{\mathscr{H}}^q(M) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}^q(M) , \]
(3.4.4) \[ \varphi_X^q(M) : \check{H}^q(X, M) \longrightarrow H^q(X, M) . \]

The morphisms \(\varphi^q\) and \(\varphi_X^q\) are isomorphisms when \(q\) equals 0 or 1. The morphisms \(\varphi^2\) and \(\varphi_X^2\) are monomorphisms. More generally, when the presheaves \(\mathscr{H}^i(M)\) are zero for \(0 < i < n\), the morphisms \(\varphi^q(M)\) and \(\varphi_X^q(M)\) are isomorphisms for \(0 \leqslant q \leqslant n\) and monomorphisms for \(q = n + 1\).

The first spectral sequence is obtained by passing to the inductive limit in the spectral sequence (3.2.1) over the sieves \(R \hookrightarrow X\) covering \(X\) (2.4.5.2). The second spectral sequence follows from it at once (2.4.5.3). The sheaves associated to the presheaves \(\mathscr{H}^q(M)\) are zero when \(q > 0\) (3.1). We therefore have \(a \circ \mathscr{H}^q(M) = 0\) for every \(q > 0\) (II 3.4). Consequently \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^0 \mathscr{H}^q(M)\) is a separated presheaf whose associated sheaf is zero. We therefore have \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^0 \mathscr{H}^q(M) = 0\) for \(q > 0\) (II 3.2). The assertions about the morphisms \(\varphi^q\) and \(\varphi_X^q\) follow from this at once.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.5

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos and \(M\) an \(A\)-Module (a left one, to fix ideas). Let \(\underline{M}\) denote the abelian Group underlying \(M\). The functor \(M \longmapsto \underline{M}\) is exact, and consequently, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), the canonical isomorphism \[ H^0(X, M) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^0(X, \underline{M}) \] extends to morphisms \[ H^q(X, M) \longrightarrow H^q(X, \underline{M}) \qquad q \geqslant 0 . \] These morphisms are isomorphisms.

For every object \(Y\) of \(E\), we have (2.4.5.4): \[ \check{H}^p(Y, M) = \varinjlim_{\mathcal{U}} H^p(\mathcal{U}, M) \qquad \check{H}^p(Y, \underline{M}) = \varinjlim_{\mathcal{U}} H^p(\mathcal{U}, \underline{M}) \] the inductive limit being taken over the epimorphic families \(\mathcal{U} = (Y_i \to Y)\), \(i \in I\).

Consequently, the canonical homomorphism \(\check{H}^p(Y, M) \to \check{H}^p(Y, \underline{M})\) is an isomorphism (2.3.4). Hence (2.4.5.3) the canonical homomorphism \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^p(M) \to \check{\mathscr{H}}^p(\underline{M})\) is an isomorphism. If \(M\) is an injective \(A\)-Module, we have \(\check{\mathscr{H}}^p(\underline{M}) = 0\) for \(p > 0\); whence \(\mathscr{H}^1(\underline{M}) = 0\) and, by induction on \(p\), \(\mathscr{H}^p(\underline{M}) = 0\), \(p > 0\) (3.4). Hence \(H^p(X, \underline{M}) = 0\) for \(p > 0\) (2.4.2.2) and (2.5). Consequently, the functor \(M \longmapsto \underline{M}\) transforms injective objects into objects acyclic for the functor \(H^0(X, \cdot)\), whence the announced isomorphism.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 3.6

Let \(G\) be a topological group and \(B_G\) its classifying topos (IV 2.5). Let \(E_G\) denote the object of \(B_G\) consisting of the topological space underlying \(G\), equipped with the left-translation action of the elements of \(G\). The canonical morphism from \(E_G\) to the final object \(e_G\) of \(B_G\) is an epimorphism; whence a covering \(\mathcal{U} = (E_G \to e_G)\) and, for every abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(B_G\), a spectral sequence \[ \text{(3.6.1)} \qquad E_2^{p,q} = H^p(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{H}^q(F)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(B_G, F) , \] which we propose to study.

1) Show that for every integer \(n\), the topos \[ (B_G) / (E_G \times E_G \times \dots \times E_G) \qquad (n \text{ factors}) \] is canonically equivalent to the topos (IV 2.5) \[ \mathrm{TOP}(G \times G \times G \times \dots \times G) \qquad (n-1 \text{ factors}) \] For every integer \(n\), let \(F_n\) denote the sheaf on the topological space \(G \times \dots \times G\) (\(n\) factors) induced by \(F\).

2) Deduce from this that the term \(E_2^{p,q}\) of (3.6.1) is canonically isomorphic to the \(p\)-th group of cohomology of a complex of the type \[ H^q(e, F_0) \longrightarrow H^q(G, F_1) \longrightarrow H^q(G \times G, F_2) \longrightarrow \dots , \] which is to be made explicit (\(e\) denotes the topological space reduced to a point).

3) Deduce from this that the cohomology of the classifying topos \(B_G\) with values in the locally constant sheaves is isomorphic to the corresponding singular cohomology of the classifying spaces used in topology, provided that, for topological spaces of the type \(G \times G \times \dots \times G\), the cohomology of the locally constant sheaves coincides with the corresponding singular cohomology (which is the case when, for example, \(G\) is locally contractible); (for the classifying spaces, one may consult [15]).
4. Acyclic sheaves

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1.

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(F\) an \(A\)-Module, and \(S\) a topologically generating family of \(E\). We say that \(F\) is \(S\)-acyclic if for every object \(X\) of \(S\) and every integer \(q > 0\), we have \(H^q(X, F) = 0\). When \(S\) is equal to \(\operatorname{ob} E\), the \(S\)-acyclic sheaves are called the flasque sheaves.

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(F\) a sheaf of \(A\)-modules on \(C\). We say that \(F\) is \(C\)-acyclic if \(F\) is \(S\)-acyclic, where \(S\) is the family of sheaves associated to the objects of \(C\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.3

Let \((C, A)\) be a ringed \(\mathcal{U}\)-site and \(F\) a sheaf of \(A\)-modules. Let \(\mathscr{H}^0 : \widetilde{C}_A \to \widehat{C}_A\) denote the inclusion functor of \(A\)-Modules into the category of presheaves of \(A\)-modules (here these are the \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves, where \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe such that \(C\) is \(\mathcal{V}\)-small). The following conditions are equivalent:

  1. i)

    \(F\) is \(C\)-acyclic.

  2. ii)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every covering sieve \(R \hookrightarrow X\), we have: \[ H^q(R, \mathscr{H}^0(F)) = 0 \quad \text{for all } q > 0 . \]

  3. iii)

    For every object \(X\) of \(C\), we have: \[ \check{H}^q(X, F) = 0 \quad \text{for all } q > 0 ; \]

i) \(\Longrightarrow\) ii): Since \(F\) is \(C\)-acyclic, the presheaves \(\mathscr{H}^q(F)\) are zero for \(q > 0\). The spectral sequence 3.2.1 then yields an isomorphism \(H^q(R, \mathscr{H}^0(F)) \simeq H^q(aR, F)\) for every \(q\). Consequently \(H^q(R, \mathscr{H}^0(F)) = 0\) for \(q > 0\).
ii) \(\Longrightarrow\) iii): clear by passing to the inductive limit.
iii) \(\Longrightarrow\) i): we prove by induction on \(q\) that the presheaves \(\mathscr{H}^q(F)\) are zero for \(q > 0\). For this, we use 3.4.2.

It follows from criterion 4.3 ii) and from 3.5 that the property of \(S\)-acyclicity depends only on the underlying abelian sheaf. In particular, a sheaf of \(A\)-modules is flasque if and only if the underlying abelian sheaf is flasque.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 4.5

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos and \(F\) an \(A\)-Module. The following properties are equivalent:

  1. i)

    \(F\) is flasque;

  2. ii)

    For every epimorphic family \(\mathcal{U} = (X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\), \[ H^q(\mathcal{U}, F) = 0 \quad \text{for all } q > 0 . \]
In 4.2, we take for \(C\) the topos \(E\) itself. The corollary then follows from the equivalence i) \(\Longleftrightarrow\) ii) of 4.2.

Injective sheaves are flasque. Flasque sheaves are \(S\)-acyclic for every topologically generating family \(S\). Flasque sheaves are not necessarily injective (take for the topos \(E\) the topos of sets). The \(S\)-acyclic sheaves are not necessarily flasque (exercise 4.1.3).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.7

Let \((E, A)\) be a topos, \(F\) a flasque \(A\)-Module, and \(X\) an object of \(E\). For every subobject \(Y\) of \(X\), the canonical homomorphism \(H^0(X, F) \longrightarrow H^0(Y, F)\) is surjective.

Let \(Y\) be a subobject of \(X\) such that the morphism \(H^0(X, F) \longrightarrow H^0(Y, F)\) is not surjective. Let \(Z\) be the object obtained by gluing two copies \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) of \(X\) along \(Y\). The object \(Z\) is covered by the two subobjects \(X_1\) and \(X_2\), and we have \(X_1 \times_Z X_2 = Y\). Let \(\mathcal{U} = (X_1, X_2)\) denote the covering thus obtained. One sees at once that \(H^1(\mathcal{U}, F) \neq 0\). Contradiction.

The property described in 4.7 does not, in the case of general topoi, characterize the flasque sheaves (exer. 4.15). It does, however, characterize them in the case of topoi generated by their opens, and in particular in the case of topoi associated to topological spaces (exer. 4.16). The terminology "flasque" adopted here coincides, in the case of topological spaces, with the terminology of [7] (exer. 4.16).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.9.

Let \(u : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) be a morphism of ringed topoi.

  1. 1)

    The functor \(u_*\) transforms the flasque \(A\)-Modules into flasque \(A'\)-Modules.

  2. 2)

    Let \(S\) and \(S'\) be topologically generating families of \(E\) and \(E'\) respectively such that \(u^*(S') \subset S\). The functor \(u_*\) transforms the \(S\)-acyclic \(A\)-Modules into \(S'\)-acyclic \(A'\)-Modules.

  3. 3)

    When \(u\) is a flat morphism (1.8), the functor \(u_*\) transforms the injective \(A\)-Modules into injective \(A'\)-Modules.

Let \(X\) be an object of \(E'\), \(\mathcal{U} = (X_i \to X)_{i \in I}\) an epimorphic family, \(F\) a flasque \(A\)-Module, and \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, u_* F)\) the Čech complex of the covering \(\mathcal{U}\). We have a canonical isomorphism \(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, u_* F) \simeq C^\bullet(u^* \mathcal{U}, F)\), using the adjunction of \(u_*\) and \(u^*\) and the fact that \(u^*\) commutes with inductive limits, and consequently \(u^*(\mathcal{U}) = (u^* X_i \to u^* X)_{i \in I}\) is an epimorphic family. Since \(F\) is flasque, we have \(H^q(u^*(\mathcal{U}), F) = 0\) for \(q > 0\), and consequently \(H^q(\mathcal{U}, u_* F) = H^q(C^\bullet(\mathcal{U}, u_* F)) = H^q(C^\bullet(u^* \mathcal{U}, F)) = H^q(u^*(\mathcal{U}), F) = 0\) for \(q > 0\). Hence \(u_* F\) is flasque.

Let us prove 2). When \(S'\) is stable under fibre products, a proof analogous to the preceding one allows us to prove 2). In the general case, we shall use the spectral sequence of the morphism \(u\) (5.3.2). Assertion 2) will not be used before 5.3.2. Let \(F\) be an \(S\)-acyclic sheaf. The sheaves \(R^q u_* F\) are the sheaves associated to the presheaves \(X \longmapsto H^q(u^* X, F)\). Since \(S'\) is a topologically generating family and \(F\) is \(S\)-acyclic, we have \(R^q u_* F = 0\) for every \(q > 0\). The spectral sequence 5.3.2 then yields, for every object \(X\) of \(E'\), an isomorphism: \(H^q(X, u_* F) \simeq H^q(u^* X, F)\), and consequently, for every \(X\) in \(S'\), \(H^q(X, u_* F) = 0\). Let us prove 3). When the morphism \(u\) is flat, the functor \(u^*\) for Modules is exact (1.8). Consequently the functor \(u_*\), right adjoint of \(u^*\), transforms injective objects into injective objects (0.2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.10

Let \(F\) be an \(A\)-Module of the ringed topos \((E, A)\), and \(G\) an injective \(A\)-Module.

  1. 1)

    The functor \(F \longmapsto \mathscr{H}om_A(F, G)\) is exact.

  2. 2)

    The abelian group \(\mathscr{H}om_A(F, G)\) is flasque.

Proof: Let us prove 1). Let: \[ 0 \longrightarrow F' \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow F'' \longrightarrow 0 \] be an exact sequence. We must show that the sequence: \[ 0 \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_A(F'', G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_A(F, G) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_A(F', G) \longrightarrow 0 \] is exact, and for this it suffices to show that for every object \(H\) of \(E\), the sequence: \[ 0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_E(H, \mathscr{H}om_A(F'', G)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_E(H, \mathscr{H}om_A(F, G)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_E(H, \mathscr{H}om_A(F', G)) \longrightarrow 0 \] is exact. Now (IV 6.12) this last sequence is isomorphic to the sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_A(A_H \otimes_A F'', G) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_A(A_H \otimes_A F, G) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_A(A_H \otimes_A F', G) \longrightarrow 0 \] and the \(A\)-Module \(A_H\) is flat (1.3.1).
2) Let us show that \(\mathscr{H}om_A(F, G)\) is flasque. Let: \[ \mathcal{U} = (X_i \longrightarrow X) , \quad i \in I , \] be an epimorphic family of \(E\), and

\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ C_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) : \dots \ar@<1ex>[r] \ar[r] \ar@<-1ex>[r] & \coprod_{i,j} \mathbf{Z}_{X_i \times_X X_j} \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & \coprod_i \mathbf{Z}_{X_i} . } \] the complex defined in 1.5. This complex is a flat resolution of the object \(\mathbf{Z}_X\), which is itself flat (1.4 and 1.3). Let us then compute the groups:

\[ H^q(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{H}om_A(F, G)) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathbf{Z}}(C_\bullet(\mathcal{U}), \mathscr{H}om_A(F, G))) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\operatorname{Hom}_A(C_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} F, G)) \]

The complex \[ C_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} F \] is acyclic in degree \(\neq 0\), since \(C_\bullet(\mathcal{U})\) is a flat resolution of a flat module. Consequently \(\operatorname{Hom}(C_\bullet(\mathcal{U}) \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} F, G)\) is acyclic in degree \(\neq 0\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.11

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos and \(F\) a flasque (resp. injective) sheaf of \(A\)-modules.

  1. 1)

    For every object \(X\) of \(E\), the \(A|X\)-Module \(j_X^* F\) is flasque (resp. injective).

  2. 2)

    For every closed subobject \(Z\) of \(E\), the sheaf of sections of \(F\) with support in \(Z\) (IV 14) is flasque (resp. injective).

Assertion 1) follows from 4.5 when \(F\) is flasque. The functor \(j_X^*\) admits an exact left adjoint \(j_{X!}\) (IV 11). Consequently, when \(F\) is injective, \(j_X^* F\) is injective (0.2). Let us prove 2). Let \(i : Z \to E\) denote the inclusion morphism. The sheaf of sections of \(F\) with support in \(Z\) is then the sheaf \(i_* i^! F\) (IV 14). The functor \(i_* i^!\) is right adjoint to the functor \(i_* i^*\), which is exact (IV 14). Consequently it transforms an injective sheaf into an injective sheaf. Let \(U\) be the open complementary to \(Z\), \(j : U \to E\) the inclusion morphism, and \(F\) a flasque sheaf. We have an exact sequence (IV 14):
(4.11.1) \[ 0 \longrightarrow i_* i^! F \longrightarrow F \longrightarrow j_* j^* F . \]

For every object \(X\) of \(E\), we have \(j_* j^* F(X) = F(X \times U)\), and the morphism \(F(X) \longrightarrow j_* j^* F(X)\) induced by the last arrow of (4.11.1) comes from the canonical injection \(X \times U \hookrightarrow X\). Since \(F\) is flasque, this morphism is surjective (4.7), and consequently the last arrow of 4.11.1 is an epimorphism of presheaves. For every object \(X\) of \(E\), the exact cohomology sequence deduced from 4.11.1 gives \(H^q(X, i_* i^! F) = 0\) for \(q > 0\), and consequently \(i_* i^! F\) is flasque.

The property, for a sheaf, of being flasque (resp. injective) localizes (4.11 1)). But it is not, in general, a property of local character (exer. 4.15). Nevertheless, it is a property of local character in the case of topoi generated by their opens, and in particular in the case of topoi associated to the topological spaces (exer. 4.16).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 4.13

Let \(X\) be a locally compact space and \(F\) a \(c\)-soft sheaf [7]. Using the local character of softness (loc. cit.), show that the restriction of \(F\) to every paracompact open of \(X\) is a soft sheaf. Show that the paracompact opens form a base for the topology of \(X\). Deduce from this that, denoting by \(S\) the family of paracompact opens of \(X\), the sheaf \(F\) is \(S\)-acyclic. Show that the sheaf of continuous functions on \(X\) is \(S\)-acyclic but is not flasque when \(X\) is not discrete.

blocks.title: Problem
blocks.html:
Problem 4.14

Study the totally acyclic topoi, i.e. the topoi such that \(H^q(X, F) = 0\) for every \(q > 0\), every object \(X\), and every abelian sheaf \(F\).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 4.15

Let \(G\) be a discrete group and \(B_G\) its classifying topos (IV 2.4). Show that for every abelian sheaf \(F\) and every monomorphism \(X \hookrightarrow Y\), the homomorphism \(F(Y) \longrightarrow F(X)\) is surjective. Let \(E(G)\) be the group \(G\) regarded as a homogeneous space under itself. It is an object of \(B_G\). The topos \(B_{G/E(G)}\) is equivalent to the punctual topos (IV 8). The morphism \(E(G) \longrightarrow e\) (\(e\) the final object of \(B_G\)) is an epimorphism. For every abelian sheaf \(F\) of \(B_G\), the sheaf \(F|E(G)\) is flasque. Deduce from this that the property of being flasque or injective is not of local character.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 4.16

We say that a topos \(E\) is generated by its opens if the opens of \(E\) (i.e. the subobjects of the final object \(e\) of \(E\)) form a generating family (I 7). Such a topos has the following property:

(P) Every epimorphic family \(X_i \longrightarrow X\), \(i \in I\), is refined by an epimorphic family \(U_j \longrightarrow X\), \(j \in J\), where the \(U_j \longrightarrow X\) are monomorphisms.

a) Do there exist topoi that possess property (P) and that are not generated by their opens? The topoi associated to topological spaces are generated by their opens. If \(E\) is generated by its opens (resp. enjoys (P)), then for every object \(X\) of \(E\), \(E_{/X}\) is generated by its opens (resp. enjoys (P)). Every subtopos of a topos generated by its opens is generated by its opens. Property (P) is not a property of local character.

b) Let \(E\) be a topos and \(\operatorname{Ouv}(E)\) the category of opens of \(E\) equipped with the topology induced. The inclusion functor \(\operatorname{Ouv}(E) \longrightarrow E\) is a morphism of sites, whence a morphism of topoi \(\Pi : E \longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\). The functor \(\Pi^*\) is fully faithful. The morphism \(\Pi\) possesses, with respect to the 2-category of topoi generated by their opens, a universal property which the reader will make explicit.

c) Let \(E\) be a topos generated by its opens and \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) the set of points up to isomorphism of \(E\). Show that \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) is small. Put a topology on \(\operatorname{Point}(E)\) and define a morphism \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E)) \longrightarrow \widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\) making \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E))\) a subtopos of \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(E)}\). For every topological space \(X\), show that every morphism from \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) to \(E\) yields a morphism from \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) to \(\operatorname{Top}(\operatorname{Point}(E))\). Show that a topos generated by its opens is equivalent to a topos \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) (\(X\) a topological space) if and only if it has enough points. Show that there exist topoi generated by their opens that are not equivalent to topoi \(\operatorname{Top}(X)\) where \(X\) is a topological space.

d) Let \(E\) be a topos possessing property (P). In order for an abelian sheaf \(F\) on \(E\) to be flasque, it is necessary and sufficient that for every monomorphism \(X \hookrightarrow Y\), the homomorphism \(F(Y) \longrightarrow F(X)\) be surjective.

e) Let \(E\) be a topos possessing property (P). Show that the property, for a sheaf \(F\), of being flasque is a property of local nature.
