f) Let \(E\) be a topos generated by its opens and \(e\) the final object of \(E\). In order for an abelian sheaf \(F\) to be flasque, it is necessary and sufficient that for every open \(U\) of \(e\), the canonical morphism \(F(e) \longrightarrow F(U)\) be surjective.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 4.17 (Flasque sheaves and change of universe)

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (for example a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos) and \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\). Let us denote by \(\varepsilon : \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \longrightarrow \widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the canonical injection between the corresponding categories of sheaves. Let \(F\) be a flasque abelian \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf on \(C\). We propose to show that \(\varepsilon F\) is flasque. We first note that for every object \(X\) of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) we have \(H^q(\varepsilon X, \varepsilon F) = 0\) for \(q > 0\). Every object \(Y\) of \(\widetilde{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) admits an epimorphic family \(\varepsilon X_i \longrightarrow Y\), \(i \in I\), where the \(\varepsilon X_i \longrightarrow Y\) are monomorphisms. We conclude that \(H^q(Y, \varepsilon F) = \varinjlim{}^q_{\varepsilon X \to Y} F(X)\). To show that these \(\varinjlim^q\) vanish for \(q \neq 0\), we may reduce to the topos \(\widetilde{\operatorname{Ouv}(C_{\mathcal{V}/Y})}\) and use the fact that, for this topos, a sheaf is flasque if it is so locally.

pages.title: 5. The \(R^q u_*\) and the Cartan-Leray spectral sequence relative to a morphism of topoi

blocks.html: 5. The \(R^q u_*\) and the Cartan-Leray spectral sequence relative to a morphism of topoi

Let \(u : (E, A) \to (E', A')\) be a morphism of ringed topoi, \(u_* : E \to E'\) the direct image functor. The notation \(u_*\) will also denote the extension to Modules of the direct image functor. The functor \(u_*\) for Modules (left Modules, to fix ideas) is left exact. Its right derived functors are denoted \(R^q u_*\), \(q \geq 0\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1
  1. 1)

    For every \(A\)-Module \(M\), the sheaf \(R^q u_* M\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(X' \longmapsto H^q(u^* X', M)\) (\(X' \in \operatorname{ob} E'\)).

  2. 2)

    The formation of the functors \(R^q u_*\) commutes with restriction of scalars.

  3. 3)

    The formation of the \(R^q u_*\) commutes with localization. More precisely, for every object \(X'\) of \(E'\), if we denote by \(u_{/X'} : E_{/u^* X'} \longrightarrow E'_{/X'}\) the morphism deduced from \(u\) by localization (IV 8), we have, for every \(A\)-Module \(M\), a canonical isomorphism

    (5.1.1) \[ R^q(u_{/X'})_* (M | u^* X') \simeq R^q u_*(M) | X' \qquad q \geq 0 . \]

Let us denote by \(\hat{u}_* : \widehat{E} \longrightarrow \widehat{E'}\) the direct image functor for \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves (\(\hat{u}_* M = M \circ u^*\)). Since \(u^*\) and \(u_*\) are adjoint, we have an isomorphism \[ u_* \simeq a \hat{u}_* \varepsilon , \] where \(a\) is the associated sheaf functor for \(E'\). Since the functors \(a\) and \(\hat{u}_*\) are exact, we have \[ R^q u_* \simeq a \hat{u}_* \mathscr{H}^q , \] which is another way of stating 1). Assertion 2) then follows from 1) and 3.5. By the definition of the morphism \(u_{/X'}\), we have a canonical isomorphism 5.1.1 for \(q = 0\). The general case follows by noting that the localization functors (IV 8) are exact and carry injective objects to injective objects (4.11).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2

Let \(u : E \longrightarrow E'\) be a morphism of topoi and \(S'\) a generating family of \(E'\). Sheaves \(M\) that are acyclic for the functors \(H^0(u^* X', \cdot)\), \(X' \in S'\), are acyclic for the functor \(u_*\). In particular, flasque sheaves are acyclic for \(u_*\).
This follows from 5.1, 1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.3

Let \(u : E \longrightarrow E'\) be a morphism of topoi and \(M\) an abelian Group of \(E\). We have a spectral sequence:

(5.3.1) \[ E_2^{p,q} = H^p(E', R^q u_* M) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(E, M) . \]

More generally, for every object \(X'\) of \(E'\), we have a spectral sequence:

(5.3.2) \[ E_2^{p,q} = H^p(X', R^q u_* M) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(u^* X', M) . \]

By the definition of the direct and inverse image functors, we have an isomorphism \(H^0(X', u_* M) \simeq H^0(u^* X', M)\). The functor \(u_*\) carries injective objects to flasque sheaves (4.6 and 4.9). The spectral sequences above are therefore spectral sequences of composite functors (0.3).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.4

Let \(u : E \longrightarrow E'\) and \(v : E' \longrightarrow E''\) be two morphisms of topoi. We have a spectral sequence

\[ R^p v_* R^q u_* \Longrightarrow R^{p+q}(v \circ u)_* . \]

We have \(v_* u_* \simeq (vu)_*\) and the functor \(u_*\) carries injective objects to flasque sheaves (4.9), hence to sheaves acyclic for \(v_*\) (5.2). We therefore have a spectral sequence of composite functors (0.3).

pages.title: 6. Local Ext's and cohomology with supports

blocks.html: 6. Local Ext's and cohomology with supports

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(M\) an \(A\)-Module, a left Module to fix ideas. The functor \(N \longmapsto \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)\), on the category of left \(A\)-Modules and with values in the category of abelian Groups, is left exact (IV 12). Its right derived functors are denoted:
In particular, we have
(6.0.2) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N) = \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N) . \]
By definition, we have canonical isomorphisms (2.1 and IV 12).
(6.0.3) \[ H^0(E, \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N)) = \operatorname{Ext}^0_A(E; M, N) = \operatorname{Hom}_A(M, N) . \]
More generally, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), we have (2.2)
(6.0.4) \[ H^0(X, \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N)) = \operatorname{Ext}^0_A(X; M, N) = \operatorname{Hom}_{A|X}(M|X, N|X) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.1
  1. 1)

    The formation of the functors \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A\) commutes with localization. More precisely, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), we have functorial isomorphisms:

    (6.1.1) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)|X \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A|X}(M|X, N|X) . \]

  2. 2)

    The sheaf \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)\) is isomorphic to the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(X \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M, N)\).

  3. 3)

    There is a spectral sequence

    (6.1.2) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_A(E; M, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p(E, \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) . \]
More generally, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), we have a spectral sequence functorial in \(X\) and in the arguments \(M\) and \(N\)
(6.1.3) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_A(X; M, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p(X, \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) . \]

By definition, we have an isomorphism (6.1.1) when \(q = 0\) (IV 12). The general case follows, taking into account the fact that the localization functors are exact and carry injective Modules to injective Modules (2.2). The functor \(N \longmapsto \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N) = \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N)\) carries injective Modules to flasque sheaves, hence to sheaves acyclic for \(H^0(X, \cdot)\) (4.10). The spectral sequences (6.1.2) and (6.1.3) are spectral sequences of composite functors, taking (6.0.3) and (6.0.4) into account. As \(X\) varies in \(E\), the spectral sequence (6.1.3) yields a spectral sequence of presheaves, whence, upon passing to associated sheaves, a spectral sequence of sheaves. Since the sheaves associated to the presheaves \(X \longmapsto H^p(X, \cdot)\) are zero when \(p \neq 0\) (3.1), this spectral sequence degenerates and yields the isomorphism announced in 2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2

The functors \((M, N) \longmapsto \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)\), \(q \geq 0\), form a \(\delta\)-functor in the variable \(M\) and in the variable \(N\). Explicitly, for every exact sequence \(0 \longrightarrow N' \longrightarrow N \longrightarrow N'' \longrightarrow 0\) (resp. \(0 \longrightarrow M' \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow M'' \longrightarrow 0\)) we have long exact sequences:

(6.2.1) \[ \dots \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N') \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N) \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N'') \overset{\delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{E}xt^{q+1}_A(M, N') \longrightarrow \dots \]
(resp.

(6.2.2) \[ \dots \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M'', N) \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N) \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M', N) \overset{\delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{E}xt^{q+1}_A(M'', N) \longrightarrow \dots ) . \]

It follows from the general properties of the functors \(\operatorname{Ext}^q\) that for every object \(X\) of \(E\), the functors \((M, N) \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M, N)\), \(q \geq 0\), form a \(\delta\)-functor in each of the arguments, whence the assertion, by letting \(X\) vary and passing to the associated sheaf (6.1).

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(M\) an \(A\)-Module, \(Z\) a closed subset of \(E\) (IV 9), \(U\) the complementary open subset. We denote by \(H^0_Z(E, M)\) the group of sections of \(M\) whose support is contained in \(Z\) (IV 14) and by \(\underline{H}^0_Z(M)\) the subsheaf of \(M\) defined by the sections of \(M\) "with support in \(Z\)" (IV 14). The functors \(H^0_Z(E, \cdot)\) and \(\underline{H}^0_Z(\cdot)\) are left exact (IV 14). The derived functors are denoted \(H^q_Z(E, \cdot)\) and \(\underline{H}^q_Z(\cdot)\) respectively and called the groups (resp. sheaves) of cohomology of \(M\) with support in \(Z\)(∗).
We have canonical isomorphisms (IV 14)
(6.3.1) \[ H^0_Z(E, M) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}_A(A_Z, M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^0_A(E; A_Z, M) , \]
(6.3.2) \[ \underline{H}^0_Z(M) \simeq \mathscr{H}om_A(A_Z, M) \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(A_Z, M) , \]
whence isomorphisms for every \(q \geq 0\)
(6.3.3) \[ H^q_Z(E, M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(E; A_Z, M) , \]
(6.3.4) \[ \underline{H}^q_Z(M) \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(A_Z, M) . \]
Note that, since \(A_Z\) is a biModule, the sheaves \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(A_Z, M) \simeq \underline{H}^q_Z(M)\) are canonically equipped with \(A\)-Module structures.

For every object \(X\) of \(E\), let us denote by \(Z_{/X}\) the closed subtopos of \(E_{/X}\) deduced from \(Z\) by localization (it is the complement of \(U \times X\)). By definition, we have canonical isomorphisms

Taking (6.3.2) into account, we have canonical isomorphisms
(6.3.7) \[ H^q_Z(X, M) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; A_Z, M) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4
  1. 1)

    The formation of the functors \(\underline{H}^q_Z\) commutes with localization. More precisely, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), and every \(A\)-Module \(M\), we have canonical isomorphisms

    (6.4.1) \[ \underline{H}^q_Z(M)|X \simeq \underline{H}^q_{Z_{/X}}(M|X) . \]

  2. 2)

    The sheaf \(\underline{H}^q_Z(M)\) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(X \longmapsto H^q_Z(X, M)\).

  3. 3)

    There is a spectral sequence:

    (6.4.2) \[ H^{p+q}_Z(E, M) \Longleftarrow H^p(E, \underline{H}^q_Z(M)) . \]
More generally, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), there is a spectral sequence
(6.4.3) \[ H^{p+q}_Z(X, M) \Longleftarrow H^p(X, \underline{H}^q_Z(M)) . \]
This is merely a translation of Proposition 6.1 by means of the dictionary 6.3.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5

With the notation of 6.3, let us denote by \(j : U \to E\) the canonical morphism. For every \(A\)-Module \(M\), there is an exact sequence of sheaves:
(6.5.1) \[ 0 \longrightarrow \underline{H}^0_Z(M) \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow j_*(M|U) \longrightarrow \underline{H}^1_Z(M) \longrightarrow 0 , \]
and isomorphisms for \(q \geq 2\):
(6.5.2) \[ \underline{H}^q_Z(M) \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^{q-1}_A(A_U, M) \simeq R^{q-1} j_*(M|U) . \]
Moreover, we have a long exact sequence
(6.5.3) \[ \dots \longrightarrow H^q_Z(E, M) \longrightarrow H^q(E, M) \longrightarrow H^q(U, M) \longrightarrow H^{q+1}_Z(E, M) \longrightarrow \dots \](∗),
and more generally, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), we have a long exact sequence
(6.5.4) \[ \dots \longrightarrow H^q_Z(X, M) \longrightarrow H^q(X, M) \longrightarrow H^q(X \times U, M) \longrightarrow H^{q+1}_Z(X, M) \longrightarrow \dots \]
By the definition of \(A_Z\), we have an exact sequence (IV 14)
(6.5.5) \[ 0 \longrightarrow A_U \longrightarrow A \longrightarrow A_Z \longrightarrow 0 . \]

The functors \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(A, \cdot)\) vanish for \(q > 0\). We have \(\mathscr{H}om_A(A_U, M) \simeq j_*(M|U)\) (IV 14) and hence (2.2) \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(A_U, M) \simeq R^q j_*(M|U)\). Finally \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(A_Z, M) \simeq \underline{H}^q_Z(M)\) (6.3.4). The long exact sequence (6.2.2) yields in this case (6.5.1) and (6.5.2). The exact sequences (6.5.3) and (6.5.4) follow from the dictionary 6.3 and from the long exact sequence of the \(\delta\)-functor \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; \cdot, M)\), \(q \geq 0\), associated to (6.5.5).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.6
  1. 1)

    Flasque sheaves are acyclic for the functors \(\underline{H}^0_Z\) and \(H^0_Z(X, \cdot)\).

  2. 2)

    The functors \(\underline{H}^q_Z\) and \(H^q_Z(X, \cdot)\) commute with restriction of scalars.

Let \(M\) be a flasque sheaf. The exact sequence (6.5.4) yields the equalities \(H^q_Z(X, M) = 0\) for every \(X\) and every \(q \geq 2\) and an exact sequence \[ 0 \longrightarrow H^0_Z(X, M) \longrightarrow H^0(X, M) \longrightarrow H^0(X \times U, M) \longrightarrow H^1_Z(X, M) \longrightarrow 0 . \] But since the sheaf \(M\) is flasque, the morphism \(H^0(X, M) \longrightarrow H^0(X \times U, M)\) is surjective (4.). Hence \(H^1_Z(X, M) = 0\) and \(M\) is acyclic for \(H^0_Z(X; M)\). Passing to associated sheaves, we deduce that \(M\) is acyclic for the functor \(\underline{H}^0_Z\) (6.4). It is clear that the functors \(\underline{H}^0_Z\) and \(H^0_Z(X, \cdot)\) commute with restriction of scalars, and since flasque sheaves are acyclic for these two functors, property 2) follows.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.7

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(Z\) a closed subset of \(E\), \(U\) the complementary open subset, \(M\) and \(N\) two \(A\)-Modules. There are isomorphisms, functorial in \(M\) and \(N\), compatible with changes of closed subset:
\[ \underline{H}^0_Z(\mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{H}om_A(M, \underline{H}^0_Z(N)) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{H}om_A(M \otimes_A A_Z, N) . \]
This follows from (IV 14), taking (6.3.2) into account.
We set
(6.8.1) \[ \mathscr{H}om_{A, Z}(M, N) = \underline{H}^0_Z(\mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) . \]

The functor \(N \longmapsto \mathscr{H}om_{A, Z}(M, N)\) is left exact. Its derived functors are denoted \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N)\): these are the \(\mathscr{E}xt\) sheaves with supports in \(Z\). We thus have
(6.8.2) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, Z}(M, N) = \mathscr{H}om_{A, Z}(M, N) . \]
Let \(M_Z = M \otimes_A A_Z\). It follows from IV 14 that \(M_Z\) is the direct image on \(E\) of the inverse image on \(Z\) of \(M\). Taking 6.7 into account, we thus have isomorphisms
(6.8.3) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N) \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M_Z, N) . \]
Let us now turn to global invariants. We set
(6.8.4) \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{A, Z}(M, N) = \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(E; M, N) = H^0_Z(E, \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) . \]

The group \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A, Z}(M, N)\) is the subgroup of the group of morphisms of \(M\) into \(N\) whose support is in \(Z\) (IV 14), i.e. which vanish on \(U\). More generally, for every object \(X\) of \(E\), we set
(6.8.5) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(X; M, N) = H^0_Z(X, \mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)) . \]

The functors \(N \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(X; M, N)\) are left exact. The derived functors are denoted \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_{A, Z}(X; M, N)\). These are the \(\operatorname{Ext}\) groups with supports in \(Z\). The definitions 6.3.6, 6.8.1 and 6.8.5, together with the isomorphisms 6.7, provide isomorphisms

(6.8.6) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(X; M, N) \simeq \begin{cases} H^0(X, \mathscr{H}om_{A, Z}(M, N)) , \\ \operatorname{Ext}^0_A(X; M, \underline{H}^0_Z(N)) , \\ \operatorname{Ext}^0_A(X; M_Z, N) . \end{cases} \]
The last isomorphism in (6.8.6) provides isomorphisms
(6.8.7) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A, Z}(X; M, N) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; M_Z, N) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.9
  1. 1)

    There are two spectral sequences, functorial in \(M\) and \(N\), compatible with changes of closed subset

    (6.9.1) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^{p+q}_{A, Z}(M, N) \Longleftarrow \begin{cases} E_2^{p,q} = \underline{H}^p_Z(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) , \\ {}'E_2^{p,q} = \mathscr{E}xt^p_A(M, \underline{H}^q_Z(N)) . \end{cases} \]

  2. 2)

    There are three spectral sequences, functorial in \(X\), \(M\) and \(N\), compatible with changes of closed subset

    (6.9.2) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_{A, Z}(X; M, N) \Longleftarrow \begin{cases} E_2^{p,q} = H^p_Z(X, \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) , \\ {}'E_2^{p,q} = H^p(X, \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N)) , \\ {}''E_2^{p,q} = \operatorname{Ext}^p_A(X; M, \underline{H}^q_Z(N)) . \end{cases} \]

  3. 3)

    The sheaves \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N)\) are canonically isomorphic to the sheaves associated to the presheaves \(X \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A, Z}(X; M, N)\).

When \(N\) is injective, the sheaf \(\mathscr{H}om_A(M, N)\) is flasque 4.10, hence acyclic for \(\underline{H}^0_Z\) (6.6). The first spectral sequence of 6.9.1 is a spectral sequence of composite functors (6.8.1). Likewise, when \(N\) is injective, \(\underline{H}^0_Z(N)\) is injective (4.11) and the second spectral sequence of 6.9.1 is a spectral sequence of composite functors deduced from 6.7. The spectral sequences of 6.9.2 are spectral sequences of composite functors deduced from the definition 6.8.5 and the first two isomorphisms of 6.8.6. Finally, letting \(X\) vary in the second spectral sequence of 6.9.2 and passing to the associated sheaves, we obtain a spectral sequence of sheaves which degenerates by virtue of 3.1 and which yields the isomorphisms of 3).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.10

The functors \((M, N) \longmapsto \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N)\), \(q \geq 0\), and \((M, N) \longmapsto \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A, Z}(X; M, N)\), \(q \geq 0\), are \(\delta\)-functors in each of the variables \(M\) and \(N\). Denoting by \(M_U\) the sheaf \(M \otimes_A A_U\) (cf. IV 11), we have a long exact sequence

(6.10.1) \[ \dots \overset{\delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, Z}(M, N) \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N) \longrightarrow \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M_U, N) \overset{\delta}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{E}xt^{q+1}_{A, Z}(M, N) \longrightarrow \dots \]
and an analogous exact sequence for the groups \(\operatorname{Ext}\).

The functors \(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(\cdot, \cdot)\) and \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; \cdot, \cdot)\) form \(\delta\)-functors with respect to each variable (6.2), and the functor \(M \longmapsto M_Z\) is exact because \(A_Z\) is flat (1.3.3). The first assertion therefore follows from the isomorphisms 6.8.3 and 6.8.7. The exact sequence 6.10.1, and the analogous exact sequence for the groups \(\operatorname{Ext}\), is the long exact sequence of the \(\delta\)-functor \[ \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(\cdot, N) , \quad q \geq 0 \quad (\text{resp. } \operatorname{Ext}^q_A(X; \cdot, N) , \quad q \geq 0) \] relative to the exact sequence \(0 \longrightarrow M_U \longrightarrow M \longrightarrow M_Z \longrightarrow 0\), taking 6.8.3 and 6.8.7 into account.

Let us briefly indicate how these results can be extended to the case of families of supports. Let \(E\) be a topos. For every object \(X\) of \(E\) let us denote by \(\operatorname{Fer}(X)\) the set of closed subsets of the topos \(E_{/X}\). This set is in one-to-one correspondence, by passage to the complement, with the set of open subsets of the topos \(E_{/X}\), i.e. with the set of subobjects of \(X\) (IV 8). The presheaf \(\operatorname{Fer} : X \longmapsto \operatorname{Fer}(X)\) is in fact a \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaf, as one immediately verifies, and is therefore representable. In other words, there is an object of \(E\), again denoted \(\operatorname{Fer}\), and a closed subset \(Z_{\operatorname{Fer}}\) of \(E_{/\operatorname{Fer}}\) such that for every \(X\), every element of \(\operatorname{Fer}(X)\) is deduced from \(Z_{\operatorname{Fer}}\) by base change along a morphism \(u_Z : X \longrightarrow \operatorname{Fer}\) uniquely determined by \(Z\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.12

We call a family of supports of \(E\) a subset \(\Phi\) of the set of closed subsets of \(E\) which possesses the following properties:

(S1) The union of a finite family of elements of \(\Phi\) belongs to \(\Phi\).

(S2) Every closed subset of \(E\) contained in an element of \(\Phi\) is an element of \(\Phi\).

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(\Phi\) a family of supports of \(E\), \(X\) an object of \(E\). We denote by \(\Phi(X)\) the smallest family of supports of \(E_{/X}\) containing the closed subsets of \(E_{/X}\) deduced from closed subsets of \(\Phi\) by the base change \(X \longrightarrow e\) (\(e\) the final object of \(E\)). The functor \(X \longmapsto \Phi(X)\) is a subpresheaf of the sheaf \(\operatorname{Fer}\). It is therefore separated.
We say that a family \(\Phi\) of supports of \(E\) is of local character if it possesses the following property:

(CL) For every epimorphic family \((X_i \longrightarrow e)\), \(i \in I\) (where \(e\) is the final object of \(E\)) the sequence of sets \[ \Phi \longrightarrow \prod_i \Phi(X_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} \Phi(X_i \times X_j) \] is exact.

Let \(a\Phi\) be the sheaf associated to the presheaf \(X \longmapsto \Phi(X)\) (6.12.1). Condition (CL) is equivalent to the condition that the canonical morphism \(\Phi \longrightarrow a\Phi(e)\) be a bijection. (cf. the construction of the associated sheaf in II in the case of a separated presheaf). To verify (CL) one may therefore restrict to a cofinal family of epimorphic families \((X_i \longrightarrow e)\), \(i \in I\).

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 6.12.3

1) Let \(Z\) be a closed subset of \(E\). The set of closed subsets of \(E\) contained in \(Z\) is a family of supports of \(E\). It is of local character.

2) Let \(T\) be a topological space and \(\Phi\) a paracompactifying family of supports of \(T\) [7]. The family \(\Phi\) is not, in general, of local character.

3) Let \(T\) be a topological space and \(p\) an integer. The family \(\Phi_p\) of closed subsets of \(T\) of Krull codimension \(\geq p\) is a family of supports of \(T\). It is of local character.

4) Let \(E\) be a topos possessing the following property: every epimorphic family \((X_i \longrightarrow e)\), \(i \in I\), is dominated by a finite epimorphic family. Then every family of supports of \(E\) is of local character. Indeed, using example 1), it suffices to show that a filtered inductive limit \(\Phi_\lambda\) of families of local character is a family of local character, which follows immediately from passing to the inductive limit in the sequence of sets \[ \Phi_\lambda \longrightarrow \prod_i \Phi_\lambda(X_i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{i,j} \Phi_\lambda(X_i \times X_j) , \] where \((X_i \longrightarrow e)\), \(i \in I\), is a finite epimorphic family. Indeed, by 6.12.2 and the hypothesis on \(E\), one may restrict to finite epimorphic families to verify conditions (CL) and, since filtered inductive limits commute with finite projective limits (I 2), the exactness of these sequences of sets is preserved under passage to the inductive limit.

5) Let \(E\) be a coherent topos (VI 2.3). Then, by what precedes, every family of supports of \(E\) is of local character.
Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos, \(\Phi\) a family of supports of \(E\), \(N\) an \(A\)-Module (a left Module, to fix ideas), \(X\) an object of \(E\). We set
(6.13.1) \[ \underline{H}^0_\Phi(N) = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} \underline{H}^0_Z(N) , \]
(6.13.2) \[ H^0_\Phi(E, N) = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} H^0_Z(E, N) . \]
Let \(M\) be a left \(A\)-Module; we set:
(6.13.3) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, \Phi}(M, N) = \mathscr{H}om_{A, \Phi}(M, N) = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, Z}(M, N) , \]
(6.13.4) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, \Phi}(X; M, N) = \operatorname{Hom}_{A|X, \Phi(X)}(M|X, N|X) = \varinjlim_{Z \in \Phi} \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(X; M, N) . \]
We have canonical isomorphisms:
(6.13.5) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, \Phi}(M, N) \simeq \underline{H}^0_\Phi(\mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N)) , \]
(6.13.6) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, \Phi}(X; M, N) \simeq H^0_\Phi(X, \mathscr{E}xt^0_A(M, N)) . \]
When \(\Phi\) is the family of closed subsets contained in a closed subset \(Z\), we have isomorphisms:

(6.13.7) \[ \begin{cases} \underline{H}^0_\Phi \simeq \underline{H}^0_Z , \\ H^0_\Phi \simeq H^0_Z , \\ \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, \Phi}(\cdot, \cdot) \simeq \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, Z}(\cdot, \cdot) , \\ \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, \Phi}(X; \cdot, \cdot) \simeq \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, Z}(X; \cdot, \cdot) . \end{cases} \]
The inductive limits defining the preceding functors are filtered. Consequently these functors are left exact. Their right derived functors are denoted:
(6.13.8) \[ \underline{H}^q_\Phi , \quad H^q_\Phi , \quad \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, \Phi}(\cdot, \cdot) , \quad \operatorname{Ext}^q_{A, \Phi}(X; \cdot, \cdot) . \]
They too are computed as inductive limits of the functors \(\underline{H}^q_Z\), \(H^q_Z\), etc., for \(Z\) ranging over \(\Phi\).
From the isomorphisms 6.13.5 and 6.13.6, we obtain two spectral sequences by passing to the inductive limit in the first spectral sequence of 6.9.1 and the first spectral sequence of 6.9.2:
(6.13.9) \[ \mathscr{E}xt^{p+q}_{A, \Phi}(M, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = \underline{H}^p_\Phi(\mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) , \]
(6.13.10) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_{A, \Phi}(X; M, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p_\Phi(X, \mathscr{E}xt^q_A(M, N)) . \]
With the notation of 6.13, we have, without any hypothesis on \(\Phi\), a functorial morphism
(6.14.1) \[ \theta : H^0_\Phi(N) \longrightarrow H^0(E, \underline{H}^0_\Phi(N)) . \]

This morphism is always injective but is not in general an isomorphism. However, if \(\Phi\) is of local character, the morphism \(\theta\) is an isomorphism, as is immediately verified. Likewise, if \(\Phi\) is of local character, we have an isomorphism
(6.14.2) \[ \theta' : \operatorname{Ext}^0_{A, \Phi}(E; M, N) \simeq H^0(E, \mathscr{E}xt^0_{A, \Phi}(M, N)) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.15

Let \((E, A)\) be a ringed topos such that \(E\) is coherent (VI 2.3), \(\Phi\) a family of supports of \(E\), \(M\) and \(N\) two \(A\)-Modules. There are two spectral sequences:
(6.15.1) \[ H^{p+q}_\Phi(E, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p_\Phi(E, \underline{H}^q_\Phi(N)) , \]
(6.15.2) \[ \operatorname{Ext}^{p+q}_{A, \Phi}(E; M, N) \Longleftarrow E_2^{p,q} = H^p(E, \mathscr{E}xt^q_{A, \Phi}(M, N)) . \]

These spectral sequences are deduced from the spectral sequence 6.4.2 and from the second spectral sequence 6.9.2 by passing to the inductive limit over the closed subsets \(Z\) of \(\Phi\), taking into account that the cohomology of a coherent topos commutes with inductive limits of sheaves (IV 5).

Let us mention, without proof, that the second spectral sequence of 6.9.1 and the third spectral sequence of 6.9.2 (with \(X\) = the final object of \(E\)) can be extended to the case of families of supports, assuming that the topos \(E\) is coherent and that the Module \(M\) is perfect [13].

Finally, one can also generalize the notion of families of supports by introducing presheaves of families of supports, sheaves of families of supports, and the corresponding groups and sheaves of cohomology(∗).

footnotes.html: (∗) Compare with SGA 2 I for the case of ordinary topological spaces, as well as HARTSHORNE's account cited p.80 below.
(∗) this exact sequence makes precise the role of the global cohomological invariants \(H^q_Z(E, N)\) as "cohomology groups of \(E\) modulo the open subset \(U\), with coefficient in \(M\)".
(∗) cf. [12] chap. IV, § 1 (Lecture Notes 20, Springer) for the development of these notions in the form of a fugue with variations.

blocks.html: 7. Appendix: Čech cohomology

Developing an idea due to P. Cartier, we show in this section how, in an arbitrary topos, one can compute the cohomology of a sheaf by means of coverings. For the classical theory of paracompact spaces, we refer to [7]; for another method which applies to certain topoi, and in particular to the étale topos, see [14].
7.1 Skeleton and coskeleton

Let \(\Delta\) be the category of standard simplices (the objects of \(\Delta\) are the ordered sets \(\Delta_n = [0, \dots, n]\), the morphisms are the increasing maps). Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos and \(\Delta E\) the category of presheaves on \(\Delta\) with values in \(E\), in other words the category of semisimplicial objects of \(E\). Let us denote by \(\Delta[n]\) the full subcategory of \(\Delta\) defined by the objects \(\Delta_p\), \(p \leq n\), by \(i_n : \Delta[n] \to \Delta\) the inclusion functor, and by \(\Delta E[n]\) the category of presheaves on \(\Delta[n]\) with values in \(E\), in other words, the category of semisimplicial objects of \(E\) truncated at order \(n\). By I 5.1, we have a sequence of three adjoint functors (I 5.3)
\[ \xymatrix@C=4em{ \Delta E[n] \ar@<1ex>[r]^-{i_{n!}} \ar@<-1ex>[r]_-{i_{n*}} & \Delta E \ar[l]|-{i_n^*} } \]

where the functor \(i_n^*\) is the restriction functor to the category \(\Delta[n]\), and where the functors \(i_{n*}\) and \(i_{n!}\) are respectively its right and left adjoints. Note that \(\Delta E\) and \(\Delta E[n]\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-topoi (IV 1.2) and that \((i_n^*, i_{n*})\) is a morphism of topoi (IV 3.1) which is an embedding of \(\Delta E[n]\) into \(\Delta E\) (I 5.6 and IV 9.1.1).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.1.1

We denote by \(\operatorname{sk}_n\) (resp. \(\operatorname{cosk}_n\)) and call the skeleton functor of order n (resp. coskeleton functor of order n) the functor \(i_{n!} i_n^*\) (resp. \(i_{n*} i_n^*\)) from \(\Delta E\) to \(\Delta E\).
The skeleton and coskeleton functors are in constant use in the theory of semi-simplicial sets [3].

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.1.2
  1. 1)

    The adjunction morphism \(\operatorname{sk}_n \longrightarrow \operatorname{id}\) is a monomorphism. The canonical morphisms \(\operatorname{sk}_n \operatorname{sk}_m \longrightarrow \operatorname{sk}_n\) (resp. \(\operatorname{cosk}_n \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_n \operatorname{cosk}_m\)) are isomorphisms when \(n \leq m\) (resp. \(n \geq m\)).

  2. 2)

    Let \(u : E \longrightarrow E'\) be a morphism of topoi. The functor \(u^*\), extended to semi-simplicial and truncated semi-simplicial objects, commutes with the functors \(i_{n!}\), \(i_n^*\), \(\operatorname{sk}_n\), \(\operatorname{cosk}_n\).

The first assertion follows immediately from the definitions. To prove 2), it suffices to note that, by I 5.1, the functors \(i_{n!} \dots\), \(\operatorname{cosk}_n\) are computed by means of inductive limits and finite projective limits.
7.2 An acyclicity lemma

Let \(M\) be an abelian group of \(E\). The homology of a semi-simplicial object \(K_\bullet\) of \(E\), with coefficients in \(M\), is defined in the usual way: we first consider \(A(K)\), the free abelian semi-simplicial group generated by \(K\), then we form the tensor product \(M \otimes_{\mathbf{Z}} A(K)\); we thus obtain an abelian semi-simplicial group of \(E\). We then consider the associated abelian group complex (by forming the alternating sum of the boundary operators) and take its homology. The homology objects are denoted \(H_i(K, M)\). These are abelian groups of \(E\). When \(M\) is the group \(\mathbf{Z}_E\) (the free abelian group generated by the final object of \(E\)), we simply write \(H_i(K)\). The groups \(H_i(K)\) are called the homology groups of \(K\). A semi-simplicial object \(K\) is said to be acyclic if for every abelian group \(M\) of \(E\), the groups \(H_i(K, M)\) are zero (\(i > 0\)), or, equivalently, if the groups \(H_i(K)\) are zero (\(i > 0\)).
The formation of homology commutes with inverse images under morphisms of topoi.
The purpose of this section is to prove the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.2.1

Let \(E\) be a topos, \(K_\bullet\) and \(L_\bullet\) two semi-simplicial objects of \(E\), \(v_\bullet : K_\bullet \longrightarrow L_\bullet\) a morphism of semi-simplicial objects, \(n\) an integer \(\geq 0\). Suppose that the morphism \(v_\bullet\) has the following properties:

  1. 1)

    For every integer \(p < n\) (\(p \geq 0\)) the morphism \(v_p : K_p \longrightarrow L_p\) is an isomorphism.

  2. 2)

    The morphism \(K_n \overset{v_n}{\longrightarrow} L_n\) is an epimorphism.

  3. 3)

    The canonical morphisms \(K_\bullet \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_n(K_\bullet)\), \(L_\bullet \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_n(L_\bullet)\) are isomorphisms.

Then, for every integer \(p\), the morphism \(v_p\) is an epimorphism and the morphism \(v_\bullet\) induces an isomorphism on the homology objects.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

The proof shows in fact that, by adopting a suitable definition of homotopy in topoi, the morphism \(v_\bullet\) is a homotopy equivalence.

Proof: We may assume that \(E\) is the topos of sheaves on a small site \(C\) (IV 1), and hence that \(E\) is a subtopos of a topos \(E'\) having enough fibre functors (for example the topos \(\widehat{C}\)). Let \(a^* : E' \longrightarrow E\) denote the inverse image functor for the embedding morphism \(E \hookrightarrow E'\). Let \[ v_\bullet[n] : K_\bullet[n] \longrightarrow L_\bullet[n] \] be the morphism of truncated semi-simplicial objects obtained by truncating \(v_\bullet\) at order \(n\). Let \(L_\bullet[n]'\) denote the image (in \(E'\)) of \(K_\bullet[n]\) under \(v_\bullet[n]\), and \(v_\bullet[n]' : K_\bullet[n] \longrightarrow L_\bullet[n]'\) the morphism induced by \(v_\bullet[n]\). Set \(L! = i_{n*} L_\bullet[n]'\), \(K! = i_{n*} K_\bullet[n]\), \(v! = i_{n*} v_\bullet[n]'\) (the functor \(i_{n*}\) is here relative to \(E'\)). By 1), the morphism \(v! : K! \longrightarrow L!\) has properties 1), 2), 3) of the lemma. Moreover, by 2), 3) and 7.1.2, the morphism \(a^* v!\) is none other than \(v_\bullet\). It therefore suffices to prove the lemma for \(v!\), and hence we may assume that \(E\) has enough fibre functors; then, using these fibre functors, we can reduce to the case where \(E\) is the category of sets.

We first observe that the hypotheses of the lemma on the morphism \(v_\bullet\) are stable under any base change \(M_\bullet \longrightarrow L_\bullet\) where \(M_\bullet\) is a coskeleton of order \(n\). Hence the fibre \(P_\bullet\) of \(v_\bullet\) at any base point of \(L_\bullet\) is of the type \(i_{n*} P_\bullet[n]\), where \(P_\bullet[n]\) is a nonempty complex truncated at order \(n\) of the form
(7.2.2) \[ P_n \longrightarrow e \longrightarrow e \longrightarrow e \longrightarrow \dots \longrightarrow e . \]

For every integer \(i\), let \(\delta \Delta_i\) denote the semi-simplicial set that is the boundary of the simplex \(\Delta_i\). Every morphism from \(\delta \Delta_i\) to \(P_\bullet\) extends to a morphism from \(\Delta_i\) to \(P_\bullet\). Indeed, the property is obvious if \(i \geq n\), since \(P_\bullet\) is a coskeleton of order \(n\), and it is clear for \(i < n\) from the description in 7.2.2. Since \(P_\bullet\) is a Kan complex, \(P_\bullet\) is homotopically trivial [6]. Note that the morphism \(v_\bullet\) is a fibration in the sense of Kan [6]. Since the fibres of this fibration are homotopically trivial, \(v_\bullet\) induces an isomorphism on the homotopy groups of \(K_\bullet\) and \(L_\bullet\) at all base points of \(K_\bullet\). By the Hurewicz theorem, this implies that \(v_\bullet\) induces an isomorphism on homology [6]. This proves the second assertion of the lemma. To prove the first assertion, we observe that every morphism from a complex truncated at order \(n\) into \(L_\bullet[n]\) lifts to a morphism into \(K_\bullet[n]\). Hence, by 3), every morphism from a complex into \(L_\bullet\) lifts to a morphism into \(L_\bullet\). Therefore \(v_\bullet\) is surjective.
7.3. Hypercoverings

Let \(C\) be a site, belonging to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\), in which fibre products and products of two objects are representable. Let \(\widehat{C}\) denote the topos of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves on \(C\) and \(\widetilde{C}\) the topos of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves on \(C\). An object \(K_\bullet\) of \(\widehat{C}\) is said to be semi-representable if it is isomorphic to a direct sum of representable presheaves.

Let \(\operatorname{SR}(C)\) be the full subcategory of \(\widehat{C}\) defined by the semi-representable objects. In the category \(\operatorname{SR}(C)\), projective limits over finite nonempty index categories are representable, and the inclusion functor \(\operatorname{SR}(C) \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}\) commutes with these finite projective limits. By a remark already made, it follows that if \(K_\bullet\) is a semi-simplicial object of \(\widehat{C}\) truncated at order \(n\) all of whose objects are semi-representable, the extension \(i_n^*(K_\bullet)\) has the same property. Hence if \(K_\bullet\) is a semi-simplicial object of \(\widehat{C}\) all of whose objects are semi-representable, then for every \(n\), the object \(\operatorname{cosk}_n(K_\bullet)\) has the same property.
7.3.1 Definitions and notation

Let \(p > 0\) be an integer. A semi-simplicial object \(K_\bullet\) of \(\widehat{C}\) is called a hypercovering of type \(p\) of \(C\), or, when no confusion can result, a hypercovering of type \(p\), if it has the following properties:
HR1) For every integer \(n \geq 0\), \(K_n\) is semi-representable.
HR2) The canonical morphism \(K_\bullet \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_p(K_\bullet)\) is an isomorphism.

HR3) For every integer \(n \geq 0\) the canonical morphism of presheaves \(K_{n+1} \longrightarrow (\operatorname{cosk}_n(K_\bullet))_{n+1}\) is a covering morphism of presheaves (II 6.2). The canonical morphism of presheaves \(K_o \longrightarrow e\), where \(e\) is the final object of \(\widehat{C}\), is a covering morphism of presheaves.

A hypercovering of type \(p\) is a hypercovering of type \(q\) for every \(q \geq p\). A semi-simplicial object \(K_\bullet\) will be called a hypercovering (of \(C\)) if it has properties HR 1) and HR3).
We shall denote by \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. \(\operatorname{HR}\)) and call the category of hypercoverings of type \(p\) (resp. the category of hypercoverings) the following category:
a) The objects of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. \(\operatorname{HR}\)) are the hypercoverings of type \(p\) (resp. the hypercoverings).

b) Let \(K_\bullet\) and \(L_\bullet\) be two objects of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. \(\operatorname{HR}\)). A morphism of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. \(\operatorname{HR}\)) with source \(K_\bullet\) and target \(L_\bullet\) is a morphism \(v_\bullet : K_\bullet \longrightarrow L_\bullet\) of semi-simplicial objects of \(\widehat{C}\).

Let \(C\) be a site in which fibre products are representable, and let \(X\) be an object of \(C\). A hypercovering of \(X\) (resp. a hypercovering of type \(p\) of \(X\)) will be a hypercovering of the site \(C/X\) (resp. a hypercovering of type \(p\) of \(C/X\)). One defines likewise the category of hypercoverings of \(X\) (resp. of hypercoverings of type \(p\) of \(X\)). We have a sequence of inclusion functors:
\[ \dots \hookrightarrow \operatorname{HR}_p \hookrightarrow \operatorname{HR}_{p+1} \hookrightarrow \dots \hookrightarrow \operatorname{HR} \]
These functors are fully faithful. We shall denote by \(\operatorname{HR}_\infty\) the inductive limit of the categories \(\operatorname{HR}_p\).

Let us denote, for every integer \(n \geq 0\), by \(\underline{\Delta}_n^e\) the standard semi-simplicial object of dimension \(n\) with values in the category of sets, i.e. the functor on \(\Delta\) represented by the ordered set \([o, n]\). We denote by \(\underline{\Delta}_n^c\) the presheaf on \(C\) (with values in the category of semi-simplicial sets) constant with value \(\underline{\Delta}_n\). The presheaf \(\underline{\Delta}_n^c\) is thus a presheaf of semi-simplicial sets. The two canonical injections of \(\Delta_o\) into \(\Delta_1\) define two morphisms of semi-simplicial presheaves:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \underline{\Delta}_0^c \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{e_0} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{e_1} & \underline{\Delta}_1^c } \]
and hence define, for every semi-simplicial presheaf \(K_\bullet\), two canonical injections:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ K_\bullet \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{e_0} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{e_1} & K_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c } \]

Two morphisms \(\xymatrix@C=2em{K_\bullet \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{u_0} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{u_1} & L_\bullet}\) of semi-simplicial presheaves are called homotopic morphisms if there exists a morphism \[ v : K_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \longrightarrow L_\bullet \] such that the diagrams:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ K_\bullet \ar[r]^-{e_i} \ar[dr]_-{u_i} & K_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \ar[d]^-{v} \\ & L_\bullet } \qquad i = 0, 1 \]

are commutative. The morphism \(v\) is called a homotopy connecting \(u_0\) to \(u_1\). The relation "\(u_0\) and \(u_1\) are two homotopic morphisms from \(K_\bullet\) to \(L_\bullet\)" is not, in general, an equivalence relation. However the equivalence relation generated by this relation is compatible with composition of morphisms. This allows us to define the category of semi-simplicial presheaves up to homotopy, by passing to the quotient by the equivalence relation generated by the homotopy relation.
We thus define the categories \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}_p\), \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}_\infty\), \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}\), the categories of hypercoverings up to homotopy.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.3.2

Let \(C\) be a site satisfying conditions 7.3.0.

  1. 1)

    The category \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}_p^\circ\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}^\circ\)) is filtered (I 2.7).

  2. 2)

    Let \(K_\bullet\) be an object of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)), \(n\) an integer such that \(0 \leq n \leq p\) (resp. \(0 \leq n\)), and \[ u : X \longrightarrow K_n \] a covering morphism of presheaves. There exists an object \(L_\bullet\) of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)) and a morphism \(f : L_\bullet \longrightarrow K_\bullet\), such that the morphism \[ f_n : L_n \longrightarrow K_n \] factors through \(u\).

  3. 3)

    The associated semi-simplicial sheaves (II 3.5) of the hypercoverings are acyclic (7.2.0) in strictly positive degrees. The \(0\)-th homology sheaf is isomorphic to the sheaf associated to the constant sheaf \(\mathbf{Z}\).

Proof: Let us prove 3). Let \(\widetilde{K}_\bullet\) be the associated semi-simplicial sheaf of \(K_\bullet\). The "associated sheaf" functor commutes with the functor \(\operatorname{cosk}_n\) (7.1.2. 2)). Hence the semi-simplicial sheaf \(\widetilde{K}_\bullet\) has the following properties:
a) The canonical morphism \(\widetilde{K}_0 \longrightarrow e\) is an epimorphism of sheaves.
b) For every integer \(n \geq 0\), the canonical morphism \(\widetilde{K}_{n+1} \longrightarrow (\operatorname{cosk}_n(\widetilde{K}_\bullet))_{n+1}\) is an epimorphism of sheaves.
Set then, for \(n \geq 0\), \(L_{\bullet n} = \operatorname{cosk}_n \widetilde{K}_\bullet\). We then have, for every \(n\), a sequence of morphisms of semi-simplicial sheaves:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{ \widetilde{K}_\bullet \ar[r]^-{u_n} & L_{\bullet n} \ar[r]^-{v_n} & L_{\bullet\, n-1} \ar[r] & \dots \ar[r]^-{v_0} & e . } \]

and for every \(j\), \(0 \leq j \leq n\), \(v_j\) has the properties of 7.2.1. Moreover, the morphism \(u_n\) induces an isomorphism on the components of degree \(\leq n\). We then deduce from 2.1, by induction on \(n\), that \(\widetilde{K}_\bullet\) is acyclic.
To prove 1) and 2) we shall introduce some terminology.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.3.3

Let \(f : X_\bullet \longrightarrow Y_\bullet\) be a morphism of semi-simplicial presheaves. We say that \(f\) is special of type \(p\) (resp. special) if:

  1. 1)

    The objects \(X_\bullet\) and \(Y_\bullet\) are canonically isomorphic to their coskeletons of order \(p\) and \(\operatorname{cosk}_p(f) = f\) (resp. no conditions on \(f\), \(X^\bullet\) and \(Y^\bullet\)).

  2. 2)

    For every integer \(n\) such that \(0 \leq n \leq p\) (resp. \(0 \leq n\)), the morphism \(\phi_{n+1}\) appearing in the diagram below is covering:

    \[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ X_{n+1} \ar[rr]^-{f_{n+1}} \ar[dr]|-{\phi_{n+1}} \ar[dd] & & Y_{n+1} \ar[dd] \\ & P_{n+1} \ar[ur]|-{p_{n+1}} \ar[dl] & \\ (\operatorname{cosk}_n X_\bullet)_{n+1} \ar[rr]_-{(\operatorname{cosk}_n f)_{n+1}} & & (\operatorname{cosk}_n Y_\bullet)_{n+1} . } \]

    (The vertical arrows are defined by the canonical morphisms \(X_\bullet \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_n X_\bullet\) and \(Y_\bullet \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_n Y_\bullet\). The object \(P_{n+1}\) is the fibre product and \(\phi_{n+1}\) is the unique arrow making the diagram commutative).

  3. 3)

    The morphism \(f_0 : X_0 \longrightarrow Y_0\) is covering.

A semi-simplicial presheaf \(K_\bullet\) is said to be special of type \(p\) (resp. special) if the canonical morphism: \[ K_\bullet \longrightarrow e \] (\(e\) being the final semi-simplicial object) is special of type \(p\) (resp. special), i.e. if \(K_\bullet\) satisfies conditions HR 2) and HR 3) (resp. HR 3)) of 7.3.1.1.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.3.4
  1. 1)

    The composite of two special morphisms (resp. special morphisms of type \(p\)) is a special morphism (resp. special of type \(p\)).

  2. 2)

    Let \(K_\bullet\) be a special semi-simplicial presheaf (resp. special of type \(p\)), \(X_\bullet \overset{f}{\longrightarrow} Y_\bullet\) a special morphism (resp. special of type \(p\)) and \(u : K_\bullet \longrightarrow Y_\bullet\) a morphism of complexes. Then the fibre product \(P_\bullet = K_\bullet \times_{Y_\bullet} X_\bullet\) is special (resp. special of type \(p\)).
The proof of this lemma is left to the reader.

Proof of assertion 2) of 7.3.2.: We may first assume that \(X\) is semi-representable. For every semi-simplicial object \(L_\bullet\), let \(\operatorname{Hom}_{(X)}(L_\bullet, K_\bullet)\) denote the set of morphisms of semi-simplicial objects equipped with a factorization \(L_n \longrightarrow X \overset{u}{\longrightarrow} K_n\). The functor \(\operatorname{Hom}_{(X)}(\cdot, K_\bullet)\) is representable. Indeed this functor transforms inductive limits into projective limits, and the category \(\Delta(\widehat{C})\) is a topos. We shall denote by \(P\) an object representing this functor. For an object \(Z\) of \(\widehat{C}\), let us likewise denote by \(j_n^*(Z)\) the object representing the functor \(L_\bullet \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}(L_n, Z)\) on \(\Delta \widehat{C}\), whose construction by \(\varprojlim\) is made explicit in III 1.1. We observe here that this construction involves only finite \(\varprojlim\)'s, from which we immediately conclude that \(j_n^*\) transforms semi-representable presheaves into semi-simplicial presheaves with semi-representable components, and covering morphisms \(Z' \longrightarrow Z\) into special morphisms (7.3.3).
By definition of \(P_\bullet\), we have a cartesian square:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ P_\bullet \ar[r] \ar[d] & j_n^*(X) \ar[d]^-{j_n^*(u)} \\ K_\bullet \ar[r] & j_n^*(K_n) } \]

By what we have just noted, the semi-simplicial objects \(j_n^*(X)\) and \(j_n^*(K_n)\) are semi-representable, and the morphism \(j_n^*(u)\) is a special morphism of type \(n\). To conclude it then suffices to apply 3.4. and the formal properties of 7.3.0.

Let \(M_\bullet\) and \(N_\bullet\) be two semi-simplicial presheaves. The functor: \[ L_\bullet \longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}(L_\bullet \times M_\bullet, N_\bullet) \] is representable. The semi-simplicial presheaf representing it will be denoted \[ \mathscr{H}om_\bullet(M_\bullet, N_\bullet) . \] The component presheaf of degree \(n\) of this object will be denoted \(\mathscr{H}om_n(M_\bullet, N_\bullet)\). We have a canonical isomorphism \[ \mathscr{H}om_n(M_\bullet, N_\bullet) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{H}om_0(M_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_n^c, N_\bullet) . \]

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.3.6

Let

\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ M_\bullet \ar[r] & N_\bullet \\ \operatorname{sk}_n \underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[u] & \underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \ar[u] } \qquad (u \text{ the canonical injection}) \]

be a cocartesian diagram of semi-simplicial presheaves. For every hypercovering \(L_\bullet\), the morphism: \[ \mathscr{H}om_0(N_\bullet, L_\bullet) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_0(M_\bullet, L_\bullet) \] is covering.
Proof. We have a cartesian diagram:

\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ \mathscr{H}om_0(N_\bullet, L_\bullet) \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{H}om_0(M_\bullet, L_\bullet) \ar[d] \\ \mathscr{H}om_0(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c, L_\bullet) \ar[r]^-{(*)} & \mathscr{H}om_0(\operatorname{sk}_n \underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c, L_\bullet) } \]

It therefore suffices to show that the morphism \((*)\) is covering. But the morphism \((*)\) is isomorphic to the morphism: \[ L_{n+1} \longrightarrow (\operatorname{cosk}_n L_\bullet)_{n+1} \] which is covering by hypothesis, Q.E.D.

Proof of assertion 1) of 7.3.2.: The product of two objects of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)) is again an object of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)) (7.3.4). To prove that the category \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}_p^\circ\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}^\circ\)) is filtered, it suffices to show that, given two morphisms of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. \(\operatorname{HR}\))
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{K_\bullet \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{u_0} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{u_1} & L_\bullet} \]
there exists a morphism \(v : M_\bullet \longrightarrow K_\bullet\) of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)) such that the morphisms:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{M_\bullet \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{u_0 v} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{u_1 v} & L_\bullet} \]
are homotopic, i.e. such that there exists \(w : M_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \longrightarrow L_\bullet\) making the diagrams
\[ (*) \qquad \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ M_\bullet \ar[r]^-{e_i} \ar[d]_-{v} & M_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \ar[d]^-{w} \\ K_\bullet \ar[r]_-{u_i} & L_\bullet } \qquad i = 0, 1 . \]

Let then, for every semi-simplicial object \(M_\bullet\) of \(\widehat{C}\) (not necessarily a hypercovering), \(F(M_\bullet)\) be the set of pairs \((v, w) : v : M_\bullet \longrightarrow K_\bullet\), \(w : M_\bullet \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \longrightarrow L_\bullet\) such that the diagrams \((*)\) are commutative. The functor \(M_\bullet \longmapsto F(M_\bullet)\) is a contravariant functor in \(M_\bullet\) which transforms inductive limits into projective limits, and which is therefore representable by a semi-simplicial object \(F_\bullet\). The object \(F_\bullet\) is evidently the vertex of a cartesian diagram:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ F_\bullet \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \ar[d]^-{\pi} \\ K_\bullet \ar[r]_-{u_0, u_1} & L_\bullet \times L_\bullet } \]

where \(\pi\) is defined by the two inclusions of \(\underline{\Delta}_0^c\) into \(\underline{\Delta}_1^c\). To prove the assertion, it therefore suffices to show that \(F_\bullet\) is an object of \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) (resp. of \(\operatorname{HR}\)), and for this, by 7.3.4.2) and the formal properties of 7.3.0, it suffices to show that
a) \(\mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet)\) is semi-representable,
b) the morphism \(\pi\) is special of type \(p\) (resp. special).

We first immediately verify that \(\mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet)\) is a semi-representable semi-simplicial object. Indeed the components of this object are computed by finite projective limits from the \(L_n\), and are hence semi-representable. Let us now verify b). First we show that, when \(L_\bullet\) is special of type \(p\), the morphism \[ \mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \longrightarrow \operatorname{cosk}_p \mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \] is an isomorphism; this establishes property 1) of 7.3.3. Next, the morphism: \[ \pi_0 : \mathscr{H}om_0(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \longrightarrow L_0 \times L_0 \] is isomorphic to the canonical morphism \[ L_1 \overset{(d_0, d_1)}{\longrightarrow} L_0 \times L_0 \] which is covering by hypothesis (\(L_\bullet\) is a hypercovering). It remains to verify property 2) of 7.3.3, i.e. to verify that \(\forall n\), in the diagram

\[ \xymatrix@C=2em@R=2.5em{ \mathscr{H}om_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \ar[rr]^-{\pi_{n+1}} \ar[dr]|-{\phi_{n+1}} \ar[dd] & & L_{n+1} \times L_{n+1} \ar[dd] \\ & P_{n+1} \ar[ur] \ar[dl] & \\ (\operatorname{cosk}_n \mathscr{H}om_\bullet(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet))_{n+1} \ar[rr]_-{(\operatorname{cosk}_n \pi)_{n+1}} & & (\operatorname{cosk}_n L_\bullet)_{n+1} \times (\operatorname{cosk}_n L_\bullet)_{n+1} } \]

(\(P_{n+1}\) being the fibre product), the morphism \(\phi_{n+1}\) is covering. Now a simple "adjoint functors chasing" argument shows that: \[ P_{n+1} \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{H}om_0(\operatorname{sk}_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c), L_\bullet) , \] \[ \mathscr{H}om_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} \mathscr{H}om_0(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) , \] and that the morphism \(\phi_{n+1}\) is isomorphic to the morphism \[ \mathscr{H}om_0(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c, L_\bullet) \longrightarrow \mathscr{H}om_0(\operatorname{sk}_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c), L_\bullet) \] coming from the injection \[ \operatorname{sk}_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c) \hookrightarrow \underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c \] Now there exists a sequence of subobjects of \(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c\): \[ \operatorname{sk}_{n+1}(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c) = M_0 \hookrightarrow M_1 \hookrightarrow \dots \hookrightarrow M_k = \underline{\Delta}_{n+1}^c \times \underline{\Delta}_1^c , \] such that for every \(o \leq i \leq k\), the morphism \[ M_i \hookrightarrow M_{i+1} \] fits into a cocartesian diagram:
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em@R=2.5em{ M_i \ar[r] & M_{i+1} \\ \operatorname{sk}_{n+1} \underline{\Delta}_{n+2}^c \ar[r] \ar[u] & \underline{\Delta}_{n+2}^c \ar[u] } \]

(We add, one after the other, the nondegenerate simplices of dimension \(n+2\) of \(\underline{\Delta}_{n+1} \times \underline{\Delta}_1\)). By 7.3.6 the morphism \(\phi_{n+1}\) is a composite of covering morphisms and is hence itself covering, which completes the proof of 7.3.2.
7.4. The isomorphism theorem

Let \(F\) be a presheaf of abelian groups on a site \(C\) satisfying condition 7.3.0. For every hypercovering \(K_\bullet\), we set: \[ H^q(K_\bullet, F) = H^q(\operatorname{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(K_\bullet, F)) \] The \(H^q(K_\bullet, F)\) form a \(\delta\)-functor on the category of abelian presheaves on \(C\), but they are not, in general, the derived functors of the functor \(H^0(K_\bullet, F)\).
We now set:
(7.4.0.1) \[ {}^r\check{H}^q(C, F) = \varinjlim_{\operatorname{HR}_r} H^q(\cdot, F) \qquad (r \text{ may be infinite}) , \]
and
(7.4.0.2) \[ {}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, F) = \varinjlim_{\operatorname{HR}} H^q(\cdot, F) . \]

The \({}^r\check{H}^q(C, F)\) (resp. \({}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, F)\)) again form a \(\delta\)-functor, since the category \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}_p^\circ\) (resp. \(\underline{\operatorname{HR}}^\circ\)) is filtered (7.3.2). Since the categories \(\operatorname{HR}_p\) are not necessarily \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, these \(\delta\)-functors take values in the category of \(\mathcal{V}\)-abelian groups, for a suitable universe \(\mathcal{V}\).
Suppose now that the presheaf \(F\) is a sheaf. Since the semi-simplicial sheaf associated to a hypercovering is acyclic (7.3.2), we have a spectral sequence functorial in \(F\) and in \(K_\bullet\):
(7.4.0.3) \[ H^p(K_\bullet, \mathscr{H}^q(F)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\widetilde{C}, F) . \]
Hence, on passing to the limit, we obtain spectral sequences:
(7.4.0.4) \[ {}^r\check{H}^p(C, \mathscr{H}^q(F)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\widetilde{C}, F) , \] \[ {}^\infty\check{H}^p(C, \mathscr{H}^q(F)) \Longrightarrow H^{p+q}(\widetilde{C}, F) . \]

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 7.4.1

Let \(C\) be a site satisfying condition 7.3.0, \(F\) an abelian sheaf on \(C\).

  1. 1)

    The spectral sequences (7.4.0.4) define isomorphisms \[ {}^r\check{H}^q(C, F) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\widetilde{C}, F) , \qquad q \leq r+1 \] and a monomorphism \[ {}^r\check{H}^{r+2}(C, F) \longrightarrow H^{r+2}(\widetilde{C}, F) . \]

  2. 2)

    We have an isomorphism of \(\delta\)-functors: \[ {}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, F) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\widetilde{C}, F) \qquad (\text{for all } q) . \]

  3. 3)

    Let \(G\) be a presheaf of abelian groups and \(F\) the associated sheaf. There exist isomorphisms of functors: \[ {}^r\check{H}^q(C, G) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\widetilde{C}, F) , \qquad q \leq r-1 , \] and a monomorphism: \[ {}^r\check{H}^r(C, G) \longrightarrow H^r(\widetilde{C}, F) . \] When \(G\) is a separated presheaf, this last morphism is an isomorphism and there exists a monomorphism: \[ {}^r\check{H}^{r+1}(C, G) \longrightarrow H^{r+1}(\widetilde{C}, F) . \]

  4. 4)

    We have isomorphisms: \[ {}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, G) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} {}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, F) \overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow} H^q(\widetilde{C}, F) \qquad (\text{all } q) . \]

Proof: It suffices to show that if \(N\) is an abelian presheaf whose associated sheaf is zero, then \({}^r\check{H}^q(C, N) = 0\) for \(q \leq r\) (resp. \({}^\infty\check{H}^q(C, N) = 0\) for all \(q\)); this follows immediately using 3.2.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 7.4.2

1) Note that for sites satisfying condition 7.3.0, the hypercoverings of type \(0\) are the ordinary coverings, and the functors \({}^0\check{H}^q\) are none other than the functors \(\check{H}^q\) introduced in (2.4.5.1).

2) Let \(C\) be a site with representable finite projective limits such that for every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every covering family \((X_i \longrightarrow X)\), \(i \in I\), there exists an \(i_0 \in I\) such that \(X_{i_0} \longrightarrow X\) is covering. One can then show that the hypercoverings of type \(p\) whose components are representable are cofinal in \(\operatorname{HR}_p\). Likewise, the hypercoverings \(K_\bullet\) such that there exists an integer \(p\) for which \(K_\bullet\) is of type \(p\) and such that the components of \(K_\bullet\) are representable, are cofinal in \(\operatorname{HR}\). (This can be proved by adapting the method of 3.5). These hypercoverings with representable components thus suffice, in the case under consideration, to compute the cohomology of sheaves associated to presheaves.

pages.title: 8. Appendix. Local inductive limits. (by P. Deligne)

blocks.html: 8. Appendix. Local inductive limits. (by P. Deligne)

The editor recommends that the reader avoid, in principle, reading this appendix. It sets out a technique that sometimes makes it possible to extend to topoi not having enough points assertions that the existence of points renders trivial. This technique yields a sheaf-theoretic variant of D. Lazard's theorem, which states that flat modules over a ring are the inductive limits of finitely generated free modules.
8.1. Locally filtered categories
If \(\mathcal{B}\) is a category and if \(p : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) is a category over \(\mathcal{B}\), we shall use the following notation
– For \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\), \(\mathcal{A}_U\) is the fibre category \(p^{-1}(U)\)

– For \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(\lambda, \mu \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}\) such that \(p(\lambda) = U\) and \(p(\mu) = V\), we set \[ \operatorname{Hom}_f(\lambda, \mu) = p^{-1}(f) , \quad \text{where } p : \operatorname{Hom}(\lambda, \mu) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(U, V) . \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.1

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a site. We call a locally cofiltered category (or locally filtered on the left) over \(\mathcal{B}\) a category \(p : \mathcal{L} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) over \(\mathcal{B}\) such that:

(\(\mathcal{L}\)0) For every \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(\mu \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_V\), there exists \(\lambda \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_U\) such that \(\operatorname{Hom}_f(\lambda, \mu) \neq \emptyset\),

(\(\mathcal{L}\)1) For every \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\) and every finite family \((\lambda_i)\) of objects of \(\mathcal{L}_U\), there exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\) and objects \(\mu_j \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_{U_j}\) such that for every \(i\) and \(j\), we have \(\operatorname{Hom}_{f_j}(\mu_j, \lambda_i) \neq \emptyset\),

(\(\mathcal{L}\)2) For every \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and every double arrow \((\phi_0, \phi_1) : \lambda \rightrightarrows \mu\) over \(f\), there exists a covering \(f_j : V_j \longrightarrow V\) of \(V\) and arrows \(\psi_j\) with target \(\lambda\) such that \(p(\psi_j) = f_j\) and \(\phi_0 \psi_j = \phi_1 \psi_j\).
This definition simplifies when \(\mathcal{L}\) is fibred over \(\mathcal{B}\): axiom (\(\mathcal{L}\)0) is then satisfied, and (\(\mathcal{L}\)1), (\(\mathcal{L}\)2) can be stated as:

(\(\mathcal{L}\)'1) For every \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\) and every finite family \(\lambda_i\) of objects of \(\mathcal{L}_U\), locally on \(U\), there exists \(\mu\) mapping to all the \(\lambda_i\).

(\(\mathcal{L}\)'2) For every \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\), every double arrow \((\phi_0, \phi_1) : \lambda \rightrightarrows \mu\) in \(\mathcal{L}_U\) can, locally on \(U\), be equalized by an arrow with target \(\lambda\).

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a site, \(\mathcal{L}\) a category over \(\mathcal{B}\) and \(\mathcal{C}\) a stack over \(\mathcal{B}\). We denote by \(\Gamma\mathcal{C}\) the category of global sections \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\mathrm{cart}}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C})\) of \(\mathcal{C}\). If \(\mathcal{B}\) has a final object \(S\), \(\Gamma\mathcal{C}\) is "nothing other than" \(\mathcal{C}_S\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.2.1

The category of local projective systems of objects of \(C\), indexed by \(\mathcal{L}\), is the category \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{C})\).

Let us denote by \(c\) ("associated constant local projective system") the composite functor \[ \Gamma\mathcal{C} = \operatorname{Hom}^{\mathrm{cart}}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}) \hookrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}) \xrightarrow{u \mapsto u \circ p} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{C}) \] When it is necessary to make the dependence on \(\mathcal{L}\) explicit, we shall instead write \(c_{\mathcal{L}}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.3

The local projective limit functor, denoted \(\varprojlim_{\lambda \in \mathcal{L}}\), is the partially defined functor right adjoint to the functor \(c\).

The functor \[ \varprojlim_{\mathcal{L}} : \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{B}}(\mathcal{L}, \mathcal{C}) \longrightarrow \Gamma\mathcal{C} \] therefore satisfies \[ \operatorname{Hom}(X, \varprojlim_{\lambda \in \mathcal{L}} X_\lambda) \simeq \operatorname{Hom}(cX, (X_\lambda))_{\lambda \in \mathcal{L}} \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.4

A \(\mathcal{B}\)-functor \(F : \mathcal{L} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) between locally cofiltered categories over \(\mathcal{B}\) is said to be cofinal if it satisfies the following two conditions:

(C\(\mathcal{F}\)1) For every \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\) and \(\mu \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{M}_U\), there exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\) and objects \(\lambda_j \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_{U_j}\) such that \(\operatorname{Hom}_{f_j}(F(\lambda_j), \mu) \neq \emptyset\)

(C\(\mathcal{F}\)2) For every \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and every double arrow \((\phi_0, \phi_1) : F(\lambda) \rightrightarrows \mu\) over \(f\), there exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\) and arrows \(\psi_j\) with target \(\lambda\) in \(\mathcal{L}\) such that \(p(\psi_j) = f_j\) and \(\phi_0 F(\psi_j) = \phi_1 F(\psi_j)\).
The composite of two cofinal functors is a cofinal functor; equivalences of locally filtered categories are cofinal (the proof is left to the reader).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.5

Let \(F : \mathcal{L} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) be a cofinal functor of locally cofiltered categories over \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\mathcal{C}\) a stack over \(\mathcal{B}\), and \((X_\mu)_{\mu \in \mathcal{M}}\) a local projective system indexed by \(\mathcal{M}\). Then the morphism of functors in \(X\) from \(\Gamma\mathcal{C}\) to (Ens): \[ F^* : \operatorname{Hom}(c_{\mathcal{M}}(X), (X_\mu)_{\mu \in \mathcal{M}}) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Hom}(c_{\mathcal{L}}(X), X_{F(\lambda)})_{\lambda \in \mathcal{L}} \] is an isomorphism, so that \[ F^* : \varprojlim_{\mathcal{M}} X_\mu \longrightarrow \varprojlim_{\mathcal{L}} X_{F(\lambda)} \] is an isomorphism, the two sides being simultaneously defined or not defined.
The proof uses the following lemma, which is left to the reader:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.1.6

If \(F : \mathcal{L} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\) is cofinal, then, for any \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) in \(\mathcal{B}\) and arrows over \(f\) \(\phi_i : F(\lambda') \longrightarrow \mu\) (\(i = 1, 2\)), there exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\), objects \(\lambda'_j \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_{U_j}\), and commutative diagrams

\[ \xymatrix@R=1.5em{ & F(\lambda_1) \ar[dr]^-{\phi_1} & \\ F(\lambda'_j) \ar@{-->}[ur] \ar@{-->}[dr] & & \mu \\ & F(\lambda_2) \ar[ur]_-{\phi_2} & } \]
\[ \xymatrix@C=3em{U_j \ar[r]^-{f_j} & U \ar[r] & V} \]
with projection \((f_j, f)\) in \(\mathcal{B}\).

For any \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\) and \(\mu \in \mathcal{M}_U\), there exists by (C\(\mathcal{F}\)1) a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\) and arrows \(\phi_j : F(\lambda_j) \longrightarrow \mu\) over the \(f_j\). If \[ \psi = (\psi_\lambda) \in \operatorname{Hom}(c_{\mathcal{L}} X, (X_{F(\lambda)})_{\lambda \in \mathcal{L}}) : \psi_\lambda : X | p(\lambda) \longrightarrow X_{F(\lambda)} \] is the image of \[ \phi = (\phi_\mu) \in \operatorname{Hom}(c_{\mathcal{M}} X, (X_\mu)_{\mu \in \mathcal{M}}) \quad \phi_\mu : X | p(\mu) \longrightarrow X_\mu , \] the diagrams \[ \xymatrix@R=2em@C=3em{ & X_{F(\lambda_j)} \ar[dr]^-{\phi_j} & \\ X|U_j \ar[ur]^-{\psi_{\lambda_j}} \ar[rr]_-{\phi_\mu|U_j} & & X_\mu|U_j } \] are commutative, so that the \(\phi_\mu\) are determined, locally, by \(\psi\); since \(\mathcal{C}\) is a stack, we conclude that \(F^*\) is injective. To prove that \(F^*\) is surjective, let us start from \(\psi\) and construct \(\phi\) such that \(\psi = F^* \phi\). The preceding construction furnishes the composite arrows: \[ \phi_{\mu, j} : \phi_j \circ \psi_{\lambda_j} : X | U_j \longrightarrow X_\mu | U_j . \] Let us check that these arrows glue, so that there exists \(\phi_\mu : X | U \longrightarrow X_\mu\) such that \(\phi_\mu | U_j = \phi_{\mu, j}\). Consider a commutative diagram in
\[ \xymatrix@R=2em@C=2em{ & U_{ij} \ar[dl]_-{g_i} \ar[dr]^-{g_j} & \\ U_i \ar[dr]_-{f_i} & & U_j \ar[dl]^-{f_j} \\ & U & } \]

To check that \(\phi_{\mu, j} | U_{ij} = \phi_{\mu, i} | U_{ij}\), it suffices to do so locally on \(U_{ij}\), which allows us, by 8.1.6 and (\(\mathcal{L}\)2), to restrict to the case where there exists a commutative diagram
\[ \xymatrix@R=2em@C=2em{ & F(\lambda_{ij}) \ar[dl]_-{F(a_{ij})} \ar[dr]^-{F(a_{ji})} & \\ F(\lambda_i) \ar[dr]_-{\phi_i} & & F(\lambda_j) \ar[dl]^-{\phi_j} \\ & \mu & } \]
lying over the preceding one. The diagram
\[ \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=2.5em{ & X_{F(\lambda_{ij})} \ar[dl] \ar[dr] & \\ X_{F(\lambda_i)} \ar[dr] & X|U_{ij} \ar[u] \ar[l] \ar[r] & X_{F(\lambda_j)} \ar[dl] \\ & X_\mu & } \]
is then commutative, and there exists \((\phi_\mu)\) such that, for every \(\phi : F(\lambda) \longrightarrow \mu\) over \(f : V \longrightarrow U\), the diagram
\[ \xymatrix@R=2em@C=3em{ & X_{F(\lambda)} \ar[dr]^-{\phi} & \\ X|V \ar[ur]^-{\psi_\lambda} \ar[rr]_-{\phi_\mu|V} & & X_\mu|V } \]

is commutative. If \(\sigma : \mu \longrightarrow \mu'\) is an arrow of \(\mathcal{M}\), we will have \((\sigma | V)(\phi_\mu | V) = (\sigma | V) \phi \cdot \psi_\lambda = (\sigma \phi | V) \cdot \psi_\lambda = \phi_{\mu'} | V\), and hence \(\phi = (\phi_\mu)\) is a morphism of functors such that \(\psi = F^*\) as required.

If \(E\) is an ordered set, we shall also denote by \(E\) the category, having \(E\) as its set of objects, such that \(\operatorname{Hom}(i, j)\) reduces to \(1\) element or is empty according as \(i \leq j\) or not.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.7

Let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a locally cofiltered category over a site \(\mathcal{B}\). There exists an ordered set \(E\) and a functor \(F\) from \(E\) to \(\mathcal{L}\) such that

(i) \(E\), regarded as a category over \(\mathcal{B}\) by means of \(p^F : E \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\), is locally cofiltered.

(ii) The functor \(F\) is cofinal.

Let \(\mathcal{L}'\) be the locally cofiltered category that is the product of \(\mathcal{L}\) and the category defined by the ordered set \(\mathbf{Z}\). The projection of \(\mathcal{L}'\) onto \(\mathcal{L}\) is cofinal, so that it suffices to prove (8.1.7) for \(\mathcal{L}'\).

If \(X\) is a finite set of arrows in \(\mathcal{L}'\), we shall denote by \(X^\circ\) the set of the endpoints of the arrows in \(X\). Let \(E\) be the set of finite nonempty subsets of \(\operatorname{Fl}(\mathcal{L}')\), such that there exists \(\lambda_X \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}'\) satisfying
a) no arrow of \(X\), except \(1_{\lambda_X}\), has \(\lambda_X\) as endpoint,
b) if \(\mu \in X^\circ\), then \(1_\mu \in X\) and \(\operatorname{Hom}(\lambda_X, \mu) \cap X \neq \emptyset\),
c) Every diagram of the type
\[ \xymatrix@R=2em{ \lambda_X \ar[r] \ar[dr] & \mu \ar[d] \\ & \mu' } \]
of arrows of \(X\) is commutative.

We order \(E\) by the relation opposite to inclusion. If \(X \in E\), and if \(\mu \in X^\circ\), there exists one and only one arrow from \(\lambda_X\) to \(\mu\) lying in \(X\). If \(X, Y \in E\) and \(X \supset Y\), let \(\lambda_{X,Y}\) be the unique arrow in \(X\) from \(\lambda_X\) to \(\lambda_Y\). The functions \(X \longmapsto \lambda_X\) and \((X \supset Y) \longmapsto \lambda_{X,Y}\) form a functor from \(E\) to \(\mathcal{L}'\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.1.8

The category \(E\) is locally cofiltered over \(\mathcal{B}\) and the functor \(\lambda : E \longrightarrow \mathcal{L}'\) is cofinal.
We must check the axioms in turn:

(i) axiom (\(\mathcal{L}\)0). Let \(f : V \longrightarrow U\) and \(X \in E_U\). There exists \(\lambda \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}'_V\) and \(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}_f(\lambda, \lambda_X)\). Moreover, we can choose \(\lambda\) such that \(\lambda \notin X^\circ\) (this is where \(\mathcal{L}' = \mathcal{L} \times \mathbf{Z}\) is used). Let \(X' = X \cup \{1_\lambda\} \cup Y\) where \(Y\) is the set of composite arrows \[ \lambda \overset{\phi}{\longrightarrow} \lambda_X \overset{\psi}{\longrightarrow} \mu \quad (\psi \in X) . \] Then \(X' \in E\), \(\lambda_{X'} = \lambda\), and \(\operatorname{Hom}(X', X) \neq \emptyset\).

(ii) axiom (\(\mathcal{L}\)1). Let \(X_i\) be a finite family of objects of \(E_U\). There exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\), objects \(\lambda_j \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}'_{U_j}\), and arrows \(\phi_{ji} \in \operatorname{Hom}_{f_j}(\lambda_j, \lambda_{X_i})\). If \(x \in X_a \cap X_b^\circ\), there exists for each \(j\) a covering \(g_{jk} : U_{jk} \longrightarrow U_j\) and arrows \(\psi_{jk} : \lambda_{jk} \longrightarrow \lambda_j\) such that \(p(\psi_{jk}) = g_{jk}\) and which equalize the double arrow \(\lambda_j \rightrightarrows x\), where one arrow belongs to \(X_a\), the other to \(X_b\). We can arrange that the \(\lambda_{jk}\) belong to none of the \(X_i^\circ\). Let us replace the \((f_j, \lambda_j, \phi_{ji})\) by the \((f_j g_{jk}, \lambda_{jk}, \phi_{ji} \psi_{jk})\), and repeat this construction for all the \(x\) in an intersection of \(X_i\). We obtain a new system \((f_j, \lambda_j, \phi_{ji})\); let us set \[ X_j = \bigcup_i X_i \cup \{1_{\lambda_j}\} \cup Y_j \] where \(Y_j\) is the set of composite arrows \[ \lambda_j \overset{\phi_{ji}}{\longrightarrow} \lambda_{X_i} \overset{\psi}{\longrightarrow} x \quad (\psi \in X_i) . \] Then \(X_j \in E_{V_j}\), and these \(X_j\) satisfy (\(\mathcal{L}\)1).
(iii) axiom (\(\mathcal{L}\)2). Trivial, for lack of nontrivial double arrows!
(iv) axiom (C\(\mathcal{F}\)1). Trivial, since the functor \(\lambda\) is surjective.

(v) axiom (C\(\mathcal{F}\)2). Let \(f : U \longrightarrow V\) and a double arrow \((\phi_0, \phi_1) : \lambda_X \rightrightarrows \lambda\) over \(f\). There exists a covering \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) of \(U\) and arrows \(\psi_j : \lambda_j \longrightarrow \lambda_X\) such that \(p(\psi_j) = f_j\), \(\phi_0 \psi_j = \phi_1 \psi_j\), and \(\lambda_j \notin X^\circ\). Let \(X_j = X \cup \{1_{\lambda_j}\} \cup Y_j\), where \(Y_j\) is the set of composite arrows \[ \lambda_j \overset{\psi_j}{\longrightarrow} \lambda_X \overset{\psi}{\longrightarrow} \mu \quad (\psi \in X) \] Then \(X_j \in E_{V_j}\), and \(F(\lambda_{X_j, \lambda}) = \psi_j\) equalizes \((\phi_0, \phi_1)\).

Suppose that \(\mathcal{B}\) is (the site of nonempty opens of) the topological space reduced to a point. A locally cofiltered category over \(\mathcal{B}\) is then nothing other than a left filtered category (i.e. such that \(\mathcal{B}^\circ\) is filtered in the sense of I 2.7), the cofinal functors corresponding to cofinal functors of left filtered categories (I 8). Proposition 8.1.7 can be restated as

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.9

For every cofiltered category \(\mathcal{L}\) there exists a cofiltered ordered set \(E\) and a cofinal functor from \(E\) to \(\mathcal{L}\).
In this particular case, the proof of 8.1.7 essentially reduces to the proof of (8.1.9) given in I 8.

Let \(q : \mathcal{C} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) be a morphism of sites and \(p : \mathcal{L} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) a locally cofiltered category over \(\mathcal{B}\). Let us denote by \(\mathcal{L}^*\) the following category:

(i) an object of \(\mathcal{L}^*\) is a quadruple \((V, U, \phi, \lambda)\) such that \(V \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{C}\), \(U \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{B}\), \(\phi \in \operatorname{Hom}(V, q^* U)\), and \(\lambda \in \operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{L}_U\)

(ii) an arrow \(f : V, U, \phi, \lambda \longrightarrow V', \phi', U', \lambda'\) is a triple \((f_1, f_2, F_3)\) with \(f_1 \in \operatorname{Hom}(V, V')\), \(f_2 \in \operatorname{Hom}(U, U')\), \(f_3 \in \operatorname{Hom}(\lambda, \lambda')\), and \(q^* f_2 \circ \phi = \phi' \circ f_1\), \(p(f_3) = f_2\).
The functor \(f \longmapsto f_1\) makes \(\mathcal{L}^*\) a category over \(\mathcal{C}\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.1.11

The category \(\mathcal{L}^*\) is locally cofiltered over \(\mathcal{C}\).
Axiom (\(\mathcal{L}\)0) is trivial. Let us verify (\(\mathcal{L}\)1):
Let \(L_i = (V, U_i, \phi_i, \lambda_i)\) be a finite family. The \(\phi_i\) define a morphism from \(V\) to the sheaf \(q^* a \prod U_i = a \prod q^* U_i\), so that there exist commutative diagrams
\[ \xymatrix@R=2em@C=3em{ V_j \ar[r]^-{f_j} \ar[d]_-{\psi_j} & V \ar[d]^-{\phi_i} \\ q^* U_j \ar[r]_-{q^*(P_{ij})} & q^* U_i } \]
such that the \(f_j\) cover \(V\).

Let \(\lambda_{ji}\) satisfy \(\operatorname{Hom}_{P_{ij}}(\lambda_{ji}, \lambda_i) \neq \emptyset\). By (\(\mathcal{L}\)1), after possibly refining \(U_j\) (and \(V_j\)), we can take \(\lambda_{ji} = \lambda_j\) independent of \(i\), and the \(L_j = (V_j, U_j, \psi_j, \lambda_j)\) satisfy (\(\mathcal{L}\)1).

Let us verify (\(\mathcal{L}\)2). Let \((f_1, f_2) : L^1 \rightrightarrows L^2\), with \(L^i = (V^i, U^i, \phi^i, \lambda^i)\) and \(f_i = (f, g_i, h_i)\). The \(\phi_i\) define a morphism from \(V\) to the sheaf \(q^* a \operatorname{Ker}(U^1 \rightrightarrows U^2) = a \operatorname{Ker}(q^* U^1 \rightrightarrows q^* U_2)\), so that there exist commutative diagrams

\[ \xymatrix@R=2.5em@C=3em{ V_j \ar[r]^-{f_j} \ar[d]_-{\psi_j} & V^1 \ar[r] \ar[d]^-{\phi^1} & V^2 \ar[d]^-{\phi^2} \\ q^* U_j \ar[r]_-{p_j} & q^* U^1 \ar@<0.5ex>[r] \ar@<-0.5ex>[r] & U^2 } \qquad (g_1 p_j = g_2 p_j) , \]

such that the \(f_j\) cover \(V\). Let \(\chi_j : \lambda_j \longrightarrow \lambda^1\) be such that \(p(\chi_j) = p_j\). By (\(\mathcal{L}\)2) applied to \((\lambda_1 \chi_j, h_2 \chi_j)\), after possibly refining \(U_j\) (and \(V_j\)), we can arrange for \(h_1 \chi_j = h_2 \chi_j\), and the \(L_j = (V_j, U_j, \psi_j, \lambda_j)\) satisfy (\(\mathcal{L}\)2).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.12

Let \(t^* : \mathcal{A} \longrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) be a locally cofiltered category over \(\mathcal{B}\), and let us equip \(\mathcal{A}\) with the topology induced by that of \(\mathcal{B}\) by means of \(t^*\). Then \(t^*\) is an equivalence of sites \(t : \mathcal{B} \longrightarrow \mathcal{A}^*\).

By construction, \(t_* : \mathcal{F} \longmapsto \mathcal{F} \circ t^*\) carries sheaves on \(\mathcal{B}\) to sheaves on \(\mathcal{A}^*\). By (\(\mathcal{L}\)0), and (\(\mathcal{L}\)1) applied to the empty family, every "sufficiently small" object of \(\mathcal{B}\) is in the image of \(t^*\) (i.e. the image of \(t^*\) is a covering sieve in \(\mathcal{B}\)), hence by the "comparison lemma" (III 4) the inclusion in \(\mathcal{B}\) of its full subcategory defined by \(t^*(\operatorname{Ob} \mathcal{A}^*)\) is an equivalence of sites, which allows us to assume \(t^*\) surjective on objects.
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a sheaf on \(\mathcal{A}^*\).

(i) Let \(f_j : U_j \longrightarrow U\) be a covering in \(\mathcal{B}\), \(\lambda^1\) and \(\lambda^2\) in \(\mathcal{A}^*_U\), and \(f_j^i \in \operatorname{Hom}_{f_j}(\mu_j, \lambda^i)\) for \(i = 1, 2\). Then \(\mathcal{F}(\lambda^1)\) and \(\mathcal{F}(\lambda^2)\) have the same image in \(\prod_j \mathcal{F}(\mu_j)\).

Indeed, let \(x = (x_j)\) be in the image of \(\mathcal{F}(\lambda^1)\). For \(x\) to be in that of \(\mathcal{F}(\lambda^2)\), it suffices that for every commutative diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=2em{ \mu \ar[r] \ar[d] & \mu_j \ar[d] \\ \mu_k \ar[r] & \lambda^2 } \] \(x_j\) and \(x_k\) have the same image in \(\mathcal{F}(\mu)\).
